articles.body:
Former New South Wales opposition leader Mark Speakman will not contest his seat at the March state election, the latest in a mass exodus of MPs under the Liberal leader who replaced him, Kellie Sloane.

In a late-night speech on Thursday, the final sitting day of NSW’s legislative assembly before the vote, Speakman said he would not contest his south Sydney seat of Cronulla, which he has held since 2011.

He is the eighth out of 24 current Liberal MPs to announce they will not re-contest their seat in March, following Jordan Lane, Mark Coure, Tanya Davies, Ray Williams, James Griffin, Alister Henskens and Mark Taylor.

The announcement comes almost a year to the day after Speakman resigned from the leadership of the opposition in a spill in favour of Sloane, who was elected unopposed.

In that time the Coalition has gone from commanding 28% of the primary vote in NSW to 23%, Sydney Morning Herald Resolve polling suggests.

Labor has gone from 37% to 30%, while One Nation, which Resolve did not start polling separately until March, is currently at 26%.

Last week, Sloane said her party would not form government with One Nation, but she did not rule out a confidence and supply arrangement. The Australian Financial Review has reported many of her MPs privately expect the Liberals to go into a coalition with One Nation.

In his speech in the dying minutes of the parliamentary term, Speakman, a member of the party’s moderate faction, warned the Liberals against becoming “Labor lite” or “One Nation lite”, saying they should stick to the values of “Menzian Liberalism”.

Referencing Pauline Hanson’s notion of “monoculture”, Speakman said Australia was “the most successful multicultural society on the planet” and was “so much better for it”.

“You know, we hear certain people say we want a monoculture, and that people who don’t support that monoculture somehow are enemies of Australia, hate Australia,” he said.

“I love Australia for its multiculturalism. Diversity is our strength. It is our strength, and we should build on that.”

Speakman, a barrister, served as environment minister between 2015 and 2017, and was attorney general between 2017 and the Perrottet government’s defeat in the 2023 election.

He was chosen as the Liberal and opposition leader after Dominic Perrottet’s resignation, a position he held until November last year.

On Thursday, he said being opposition leader “is often said to be the toughest job in politics” and, while it had “ultimately unravelled” for him, he had mostly led an opposition “which was competitive with, or even ahead of, the government in the polls”.

He said his record as attorney general included legislating for NSW to be the first Australian jurisdiction to criminalise coercive control, introducing affirmative consent tests in criminal sexual assault trials and reforming criminal and civil child sexual abuse cases.

Speakman’s resignation, ending speculation that bubbled up again when he spoke during question time on Thursday, is the latest blow for Sloane, who he said in his leaving speech had the “attributes to be a great premier”.

In a statement on Friday morning, Sloane thanked Speakman for his “extraordinary contribution to the people of Cronulla and to NSW”.

“Since his election in 2011, Mark has been a dedicated local member, a thoughtful colleague and a principled leader of the NSW Liberal Party,” she said.

“Mark has been a generous and supportive colleague. I’m grateful for the confidence he placed in me when I became leader, and for the contribution he continues to make to our team.”

Earlier on Thursday, the NSW premier, Chris Minns, announced former Liberal councillor and parliamentary staffer Tanya Raffoul would contest the Liberal-held seat of Epping as a Labor candidate.

articles.title: Ahead of Malaysia’s next general election, BN reminds PN it won’t play second fiddle
articles.summary: Barisan Nasional is not committing to any electoral pact yet as it negotiates seat allocations with Perikatan Nasional, say analysts.
articles.preview: analysis Asia Barisan Nasional is not committing to any electoral pact yet as it negotiates seat allocations with Perikatan Nasional, say analysts. KUALA LUMPUR: After convincing wins alongside the opposition Perikatan Nasional (PN) coalition in the Melaka and Negeri Sembilan state elections, Barisan Nasional (BN) chairman Ahmad Zahid Hamidi’s comments on the pact’s future heading into the next general election might have raised a few eyebrows.
articles.body:
analysis Asia

Barisan Nasional is not committing to any electoral pact yet as it negotiates seat allocations with Perikatan Nasional, say analysts.

KUALA LUMPUR: After convincing wins alongside the opposition Perikatan Nasional (PN) coalition in the Melaka and Negeri Sembilan state elections, Barisan Nasional (BN) chairman Ahmad Zahid Hamidi’s comments on the pact’s future heading into the next general election might have raised a few eyebrows.

While BN and PN avoided direct clashes in the two recent state polls under a “political understanding”, BN had “never planned to take this (cooperation) any further”, Zahid said on Sunday (Nov 15).

“However, if the time comes and circumstances require it, we will sit down together to discuss the matter,” he said as quoted by local media.

Zahid’s comments come at a critical juncture. He has appeared to arrest BN’s decline since its dismal performance at the previous general election in 2022, just as there will likely not be further opportunities to test electoral partnerships.

After Sarawak heads to the polls on Dec 12, no other state must hold an election until the 16th general election (GE16), due by February 2028. The states of Perak, Pahang and Perlis could, however, choose to call early polls before GE16.

Analysts say BN is keeping all options on the table when it comes to partnerships for GE16, including sticking to its current arrangement within the unity government with Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim’s weakened Pakatan Harapan (PH) coalition if the latter lets BN contest more seats.

PH ceded control of Negeri Sembilan and lost ground in Johor and Melaka to BN-PN at the respective state elections.

BN chief Zahid is deputy prime minister in Anwar’s Cabinet.

But the analysts believe BN is still likely to work with PN at GE16, with BN buying time to discuss seat allocations in traditionally conservative states like Perlis, Kedah, Terengganu and Kelantan where PN is more dominant.

Ahmad Fauzi Abdul Hamid, a political science professor at Universiti Sains Malaysia (USM), said Zahid is “doing what he can to secure the most powerful position” for BN in whichever alliance it goes with for GE16.

“Zahid won’t be content playing second fiddle to PN or PH; he has clearly used the results of the Johor, Negeri Sembilan and Melaka elections to make his position clear,” he told CNA.

“Whoever is fated to collaborate with BN in GE16 will have to accept a BN prime minister - this will be the condition.”

Shifting tides of Malaysian politics

At Malaysia’s last general election in 2022, the once-dominant Barisan Nasional (BN) coalition emerged looking like a truly spent force.

Led by the United Malays National Organisation (UMNO), BN won only 30 of the 179 seats it contested, faring even worse than its performance in the 2018 general election, when the long-ruling coalition was defeated for the first time on the back of a national corruption scandal.

But royal intervention after the hung parliament in 2022 meant BN somehow clung onto power, as it joined forces with Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim’s Pakatan Harapan (PH) coalition and Borneo-based parties to form a federal unity government.

Still, PH-BN lost further ground in subsequent state elections in 2023 as Malay voters - BN’s traditional vote bank - flocked to the opposition PN, and observers questioned if BN had lost its political relevance.

Even at the Sabah state election in December 2025, where racial politics are less pronounced, PH components Parti Keadilan Rakyat (PKR) - led by Anwar - and the Chinese-majority Democratic Action Party (DAP) performed poorly. The latter failed to win a single seat of the eight it contested there, despite being the incumbent in six of them.

The results showed that DAP could be losing support among its traditional minority base, as these voters expressed frustration with Anwar’s perceived slow pace of promised reforms, analysts said then.

Fast forward to 2026, and the tide has turned. While PH’s fortunes have continued on a downward trend, BN has appeared to reverse its decline.

Zahid has orchestrated a seemingly dual track where BN maintains support for PH at the federal government level, but teams up with PN to immense success at a trio of state elections in 2026.

In an unofficial pact, the BN-PN partnership swept to victory at the Johor state election in July, and followed up by contesting the Negeri Sembilan and Melaka polls in a more official alliance, achieving equally convincing wins.

The partners achieved a two-third supermajority in all three state legislative assemblies - a feat that allows them to amend the state constitution.

Sentiments from leaders in both camps have indicated that they will continue this partnership at the next general election due by February 2028, in a bid to wrest control of Putrajaya.

ALL NOT LOST FOR UNITY GOVERNMENT PACT?

Zahid’s comments show that BN could still be willing to work with PH for GE16, something that might be used as a bargaining chip during seat negotiations with PN, said Nusantara Academy for Strategic Research senior fellow Azmi Hassan.

Going by the results of the previous general election in 2022, PN has more members of parliament than BN not only in Perlis, Kedah, Terengganu and Kelantan, but also in states with a significant PH presence like Penang, Perak and Selangor.

“If the incumbency formula is used, as in the Melaka state election, BN will be on the losing end,” Azmi told CNA, referring to a criteria parties use when dividing which seats to contest.

“It is also a message to Datuk Seri Anwar: All is not lost, because the cooperation between BN and PH still can materialise … If BN is on the losing side, BN will choose a partner that allows it to get the best outcome.”

Zahid might also stop short of finalising a deal with PN as a “better offer might come from Anwar and PH in an attempt to salvage his beleaguered government”, USM’s Fauzi said.

If this is the case, Zahid and BN would probably be content to work with PH and forgo seats in Kedah, Kelantan and Terengganu as “collateral damage”, as long as BN can secure the “most advantageous” position in any upcoming alliance, he said.

“In politics, sometimes there’s utility in being vague. By not committing himself and BN-UMNO to any future alliances, he’s keeping options open,” Fauzi added, referring to the BN lynchpin party United Malays National Organisation.

BN LIKELY TO CONTINUE WITH PN

While another political analyst agreed that Zahid was keeping options open, she feels it would be “folly” for BN not to work with PN, as this would again split the crucial Malay vote at the expense of BN.

“BN wants to contest more seats especially in Kedah and Terengganu. They’re hoping to have some leverage in negotiating with PAS,” International Islamic University Malaysia’s (IIUM) Syaza Shukri told CNA, referring to the Parti Islam Se-Malaysia component that leads PN.

“But BN knows they can’t go alone in the other states. I think it is more to buy time as they really settle seat negotiations and more importantly craft the narrative to sell to the people.”

At the 2022 general election, BN, PN and PH contested separately. By the end of campaigning, “it was evident” that PN led BN in the contest for Malay votes, an ISEAS-Yusof Ishak Institute study published in 2023 said.

Because the Malay votes were split, the post-election manoeuvrings “led to a somewhat paradoxical situation” where PH gained the right to lead the government, the study noted.

Adib Zalkapli of strategic consultancy Viewfinder Global Affairs said Zahid’s statement does not rule out future cooperation with PN.

“There are steps to be taken before firming up the cooperation, and one of the important parts of the process is seat allocation negotiations especially in the east coast states (of Terengganu and Kelantan) where PAS dominates the political landscape,” he told CNA.

Another factor that could complicate seat negotiations, he said, is the presence of PN component Parti Wawasan Negara (Wawasan), a splinter party of former PN component Parti Pribumi Bersatu Malaysia (Bersatu) largely made up of former UMNO members.

While PAS and UMNO have carved out their own areas of influence, Adib feels Wawasan is “directly competing” with UMNO.

“PAS is a pragmatic party so they have to strike a balance in the cooperation with UMNO and Wawasan,” he said.

“Despite these issues, their objective is clear - winning Putrajaya - so I believe they will set aside their differences in time before the next general election.”

Ultimately, Adib believes PAS “on paper” is content to play second fiddle to UMNO in the broader alliance.

“They know they don’t have an acceptable prime minister candidate, so the next best thing is to have a PM they can control,” he added.

WILL PAS NEGOTIATE?

Despite that, there are already signs that PAS could stand its ground with UMNO.

PN chairman Ahmad Samsuri Mokhtar, himself touted as a future prime minister candidate, said on Monday that his party PAS is open to discussing seat allocations with BN if Terengganu holds a state election.

But this only applies to the five seats in the Terengganu state legislative assembly held by PAS’ erstwhile partner Bersatu, he said according to local media. The remaining 27 seats all belong to PAS.

"Everyone knows the Terengganu assembly has 32 seats and only five seats are not from PAS. I don’t think there's any other space,” the Terengganu chief minister reportedly said.

"So, it will be up to discussions between PN and BN how to allocate these five seats.”

When asked to comment on Zahid’s statement about cooperation with PN, PN information chief Annuar Musa, who is from PAS, told CNA: “No need to respond. Not through media.”

IIUM’s Syaza said PAS is well aware that it does not need to depend on BN in states like Perak and Selangor.

“Maybe we might see some protests (to UMNO’s demands), especially by PAS youth as well, but overall I think PAS understands what is going on,” she said.

“And with Wawasan mediating, I think PAS is prepared to negotiate as well.”

Fauzi from USM suggested that UMNO and PAS need each other equally, highlighting that BN controls the southern states of Johor, Melaka and Negeri Sembilan, while PN dominates the northern states of Kedah, Terengganu and Kelantan.

Fauzi expects BN and PN to cooperate at GE16, and are only delaying announcing an official pact as BN would face "unbearable" pressure to leave Anwar’s government otherwise.

“BN and PN know that if both forces collaborate for GE16, they’ll probably be unbeatable in these states,” he added.

“So, their need for each other is now mutual. Contesting separately will benefit PH rather than either of them by splitting the Malay and anti-PH votes.”

articles.summary: Iranian foreign ministry spokesperson slams US claims about Iran's nuclear weapons Iran’s foreign ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baghaei has slammed US claims indicating "Iran is developing biological or chemical weapons". Baghaei compared the claims to "the alleged threat posed by Iraq’s weapons of mass destruction", which was proven to be untrue. "Unsubstantiated intelligence claims about Iraq’s possession of WMDs were deliberately weaponized to manufacture public support and pave the way for a military invasion," he added in a post on X. "The allegations keep changing, but the underlying narrative remains disturbingly familiar," he wrote. "The question is: has the world learned anything from the disastrous lessons of 2003, or are we about to let them deceive the public on a grand scale all over again?" After the grand narrative of the “Iranian nuclear threat,” U.S. officials are now claiming that there are indications Iran is developing biological or chemical weapons! The allegations keep changing, but the underlying narrative remains disturbingly familiar. Once again, the world is apparently expected to suffer a bout of collective amnesia - much like Dory, the forgetful fish from Finding Nemo. Do American officials really expect the world to forget Colin Powell’s infamous appearance before the UN Security Council in 2003, when he held up a small vial as a visual representation of the alleged threat posed by Iraq’s weapons of mass destruction? That moment has since become an enduring symbol of one of the most consequential intelligence failures and political deceptions in modern history. Unsubstantiated intelligence claims about Iraq’s possession of WMDs were deliberately weaponized to manufacture public support and pave the way for a military invasion. The consequences were catastrophic - not only for the Iraqi people, but for the wider region and, ultimately, for American society itself. And now we find ourselves facing ominous new allegations and a narrative that appears to be following the same fraudulent script. The question is: has the world learned anything from the disastrous lessons of 2003, or are we about to let them deceive the public on a grand scale all over again? — Esmaeil Baqaei (@IRIMFA_SPOX) November 19, 2026

articles.title: 'Humanitarian mission' for Kostiantynivka: Is it a trap?
articles.summary: Russian President Putin has proposed an evacuation of the Ukrainian city of Kostiantynivka, like the recent operation in Oleshky. Experts warn this could serve military, not humanitarian, aims. What should Kyiv do?

articles.body:
November 19, 2026

Russian President Putin has proposed an evacuation of the Ukrainian city of Kostiantynivka, like the recent operation in Oleshky. Experts warn this could serve military, not humanitarian, aims. What should Kyiv do?

Russian President Vladimir Putin has proposed a humanitarian mission in the city of Kostiantynivka similar to a recent operation in Oleshky. According to Putin, Russia has control of the city in the Donbas; the remaining civilian population, he says, could be evacuated. It would take five days to clear the access roads. The Russian leader has suggested that human rights organizations from Ukraine and Russia and delegates from the foreign press be incorporated into the mission.

Putin's proposal comes after discussions between the Russian government and US representatives, who have been negotiating to try to bring an end to Russia's war against Ukraine. Experts say that while Russia is indicating a readiness to make agreements, at the same time it is propagating its own depiction of the situation on the front line.

In July, Russia announced that it had taken Kostiantynivka but did not provide any proof. Ukraine says the fighting there is still ongoing. Experts from the Ukrainian open-source interactive map of military operations project DeepState say that the city is still controlled by the Ukrainian army, but that the situation there is "extremely difficult."

Responding to the proposal, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy told journalists: "Putin simply wants us to leave Kostiantynivka so that they can move in and occupy the entire city." He emphasized that Ukraine had always given the civilian population in Kostiantynivka opportunities to leave, and said that Russia had used the temporary ceasefire in Oleshky to bring military equipment and weapons into the city.

What is the situation for civilians?

Kostiantynivka is the southernmost city in the so-called Donetsk "fortress belt," which also includes Druzhkivka, Kramatorsk and Sloviansk. Taking Kostiantynivka would open the way for Russian troops to advance to Druzhkivka, and on to the conurbation of Sloviansk and Kramatorsk.

Oleksandr Kovalenko, a military expert at the Dmytro Tymchuk Center for Security Studies, a Ukrainian think tank, said Kostiantynivka's role is similar to that of Bakhmut, Avdiivka or Chasiv Yar — towns whose defensive installations were able to hold back Russian enemy forces for years.

Local authorities say the humanitarian situation in the city, whose population before the start of Russia's full-scale invasion was around 70,000, is catastrophic and that some 340 civilians remain. They add thatKostiantynivkahas no central water, electricity or gas supplies, there is no public transport, and since the spring of 2026 people have only been able to evacuate on foot.

"Those who stayed in Kostiantynivka need to be evacuated, they need a chance of a better life," military analyst Denys Popovych told DW. However, he added that an evacuation was virtually impossible without a ceasefire, as Russian troops had occupied the road between the town and Druzhkivka and drones were being deployed throughout the region. Ukraine, therefore, could not carry out such an operation unilaterally. "It still takes two to tango — to evacuate the people, that is," he said.

Humanitarian proposals as leverage

Kovalenko believes that Moscow is simply using the humanitarian issue for purposes of manipulation and to strengthen its negotiating position. The Russian army, he said, wants to gain time in order to reinforce units fighting in the vicinity.

Yevhen Zakharov, the director of the Kharkiv Human Rights Protection Group, has similar concerns. "I'm afraid that this proposal by the Russians has very different objectives to those they claim to pursue," he told DW. He described Putin's initiative as suspect, and said the Ukrainian side should treat it with the utmost caution.

Kyiv is in a difficult position, as the idea of a mission for Kostiantynivka is also being pushed by US intermediaries. "If we reject it, they'll say to us: 'You're rejecting peace proposals, you're not taking care of your own citizens, why should we keep talking to you, Zelenskyy wants to continue the war.' This is precisely the calculation behind it all," said Popovych.

Ceasefire as military tactic

After the end of the ceasefire in Oleshky, which was in place from October 27 to November 1, the Ukrainian General Staff announced that, in that time, the Russians had rotated their troops, entrenched their positions, reinforced measures to repel drones and brought in ammunition.

Kovalenko is convinced that the reason Russia is proposing a ceasefire is because its army is gradually losing ground in Kostiantynivka. From Moscow's perspective, the Russian troops that are meant to be storming the city are in urgent need of reinforcements, which they can't get because of the fighting on the ground.

"If a so-called humanitarian mission were to take place in Kostiantynivka, it would be a disaster for Kyiv, because Russia would use that time to consolidate forces that would enable it to take the city," he warned.

How should Kyiv respond to Moscow's proposal?

Popovych, however, does not think Ukraine should reject the Russian proposal. In his view, Kyiv should base its tactics on experiences with previous ceasefires and insist on very clear conditions in advance. "If there is a ceasefire, soldiers currently at their posts should stay there and not move," he suggested.

Oleksandr Pavlichenko from the Ukrainian Helsinki Human Rights Union believes Ukraine should submit a counter-proposal, which envisages the withdrawal of Russian troops from the Ukrainian city and the unimpeded departure of the civilian population.

The human rights activist said that, for a genuine humanitarian mission to be put in place, a strong, neutral third party should be brought in to supervise and ensure safe passage. In his view, the only party with such a mandate is the International Committee of the Red Cross. "If a proposal comes from only one side, and from a side such as Russia, it doesn't inspire confidence," he said.

This article was originally written in Ukrainian.

This week, Iraqi security forces surrounded an area run by the Kataib Hezbollah militia. Onlookers describe it as the most dangerous confrontation between the Iraqi state and Iran-allied militias in decades.

For years, there have all kinds of rumors about Jurf al-Sakhar, an area around 50 kilometers (31 miles) south of the Iraqi capital Baghdad. It is controlled by an Iraqi militia called Kataib Hezbollah, that's closely allied with Iran, and no Iraqi government troops or news media outlets have been allowed inside for around 12 years.

Rumors about what's happening in the area include allegations about secret prisons, mass graves, drone and weapons manufacturing and storage, as well as criminal activity such as oil smuggling. Jurf al-Sakhar is also allegedly a base for foreign, Hezbollah-supporting nationals from Iran, Yemen, Bahrain and Lebanon.

Recently two people — an Israeli researcherand a US journalist — who were kidnapped by an Iraqi militia are thought to have been held captive in this area.

Jurf al-Sakhar previously had an estimated 89,000 residents but after the extremist group known as the "Islamic State," or IS, rose to power in Iraq in 2014, much of the population was displaced in fighting. The area was eventually taken over by Kataib Hezbollah, a militia that had fought IS alongside other armed groups.

As a collective, the armed groups are referred to as the Popular Mobilization Forces, or PMF. Not all of them have pledged allegiance to Iran but Kataib Hezbollah, a Shiite Muslim majority group, has.

In the past 12 years, tens of thousands of the displaced people from here, mostly Sunni Muslims, have not been allowed to return and the area has been described as militarized.

Its name was even changed by Kataib Hezbollah fighters, from Jurf al-Sakhar ("rocky bank") to Jurf al-Nasr ("bank of victory").

'Not even over our dead bodies'

But recent events may shake Kataib Hezbollah's hold on this area.

An early November report for the Iraqi government says that since 2021, the group has smuggled hundreds of millions of dollars' worth of state-owned oil, siphoned from pipelines around Jurf al-Sakhar.

Kataib Hezbollah denies this.

Iraq's new government, headed by Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi, made several arrests based on the report and demanded that Kataib Hezbollah leave Jurf al-Sakhar by Friday, Nov. 20.

Kataib Hezbollah rejected al-Zaidi's ultimatum, with a spokesperson saying the group would not withdraw "not even over our dead bodies."

Al-Zaidi then ordered state security forces to surround the area, while Hezbollah reportedly brought in reinforcements.

Observers have described the standoff as one of the most consequential and riskiest confrontations between an Iraqi government and Iranian-backed militiasin Iraq in more than two decades.

"It is a political signal that things will change, that he [al-Zaidi] wants to disarm militias, integrate them into state and claim back the state's authority," Ulf Laessing, head of the Syria and Iraq project for Germany's Konrad Adenauer Foundation, or KAS, told DW. "But it's a minefield and he needs to navigate carefully."

The standoff is also the result of long-running political tensions in Iraq, where the state is torn between its US allies on the one hand and Iranian allies on the other. Both hold sway in Iraq and are considered important relationships.

During Donald Trump's presidency of the US, and thanks to the US and Israel's war with Iran, there's been more pressure on Iraq to disarm Iran's allies inside the country. Al-Zaidi has set a deadline of next June to bring all weapons under the state's control.

Tensions, fears grow

The situation in Jurf al-Sakhar became even more tense this week. Al-Zaidi announced a new security plan for the area that involves other members of the PMF, state security forces and the police. Kataib Hezbollah rejected the plan.

"Al-Zaidi appears serious about ending Kataib Hezbollah's autonomous control of Jurf al-Sakhar," Hayder al-Shakeri, a research fellow at the British think tank Chatham House told DW. "Deploying federal forces and now establishing a new security command there shows this has moved beyond rhetoric."

But how dangerous is Kataib Hezbollah really? After all, al-Zaidi was actually nominated for the prime minister's job by a political bloc known as the Coalition Framework, or CF — these are the politicians who represent the PMF in parliament. Kataib Hezbollah's political party, Harakat Huqooq, is part of the CF.

And other researchers have been critical on social media, noting that the PMF troops that will be given partial control over Jurf al-Sakhar (should Kataib Hezbollah withdraw) are associated with that group anyway.

But Iraqi news media have also reported that there are divisions inside the CF, and apparently even within Kataib Hezbollah, about how to deal with the current standoff. Reportedly, some senior officials think that parts of Jurf al-Sakhar could be handed to federal forces in a gradual withdrawal, the London-based outlet Amwaj Media reported earlier this week, while some senior members of Kataib Hezbollah would seemingly prefer to hand the territory over to certain PMF brigades rather than to state security forces.

What will happen next?

Late Thursday afternoon, the news agency Reuters reported that, according to three anonymous officials, all parties had come to an agreement that would allow government forces to enter Jurf al-Sakhar on Friday.

A compromise is good because it avoids violence, KAS' Laessing said. "It might not be what al-Zaidi initially hoped for but it's still a political signal."

If it did come to actual fighting, the Iraqi military has more resources than Kataib Hezbollah, al-Shakeri explained. "[It] could probably take Jurf al-Sakhar if the political leadership and security institutions remained united," he said. "But there would be no easy victory. Kataib Hezbollah does not need to defeat the Iraqi army conventionally. It can impose costs through asymmetric attacks, political pressure and its networks inside the state."

How the reported compromise plays out in the coming days, will also impact other Iraqi militias and they will be watching closely. Because "the core issue is whether a faction can continue controlling territory and economic activity beyond effective government oversight," al-Shakeri explained.

"The most likely compromise may be to remove Kataib Hezbollah's monopoly rather than remove the PMF from Jurf al-Sakhar altogether," he continued. "That would still matter if it opened the area to regular state forces, if it protects the oil infrastructure and places security under a clearer government command structure."

It could also lead to displaced residents being allowed back to their homes.

"But if one PMF faction simply replaces another while retaining its own networks and autonomy, then Zaidi has redistributed armed influence rather than fundamentally resolved the problem," al-Shakeri concluded.

articles.title: Ukraine allies warn ‘Yalta format’ will not bring about peace – as it happened
articles.summary: Berlin meeting of the ‘coalition of the willing’ comes after Trump declared Putin a ‘friend’ during trilateral meeting with Xi in China For what it’s worth, the China-US-Russia ‘peace declaration’ issued after their meeting, and published by Chinese state media , includes absolutely no mention of Ukraine or Europe whatsoever. There is only one, rather generic, line that could be seen as close to these issues: “The three heads of state exchanged in-depth views on the current international situation and pledged to maintain strategic stability and international security.” Continue reading...

articles.body:
'A Yalta format will not bring about peace,' Merz warns

Merz is the first to speak.

He says the leaders want “a peace for Ukraine that is both just and lasting,” with “more, not less, security for Europe and the world.”

“We will continue to support Kyiv for as long as is necessary. Should peace negotiations take place, we will be involved. Negotiations can only succeed if Ukraine and Europe are part of the process together. A “Yalta-style” format will not bring about peace.”

He says that as a gift he gave each of the guests a piece of the Berlin Wall, as an example of “what the Yalta arrangement represented for Berlin.”

“You may recall that in 1987, President Reagan stood here in Berlin and said: ‘Mr. Gorbachev, tear down this wall!’ Today, we say to President Putin: ‘end the war in Ukraine, and let us work together to find diplomatic solutions.’ We never again want to live in a divided Europe. We want to live in freedom and in peace – together.”

And, on that note, we will be closing the blog for today.

European leaders showed a united and defiant front as they repeated their backing for Ukraine “for as long as it takes” at the latest summit of the Coalition of the Willing in Berlin, declaring no decisions on Ukraine and Europe can be made without their participation (17:58, 18:06, 18:11).

Their comments appeared to play down the importance of Donald Trump’s summit with Russia’s Vladimir Putin and China’s Xi Jinping in Shenzhen (16:34), with German chancellor Friedrich Merz saying “a Yalta format will not bring about peace,” in a reference to secretive discussions between superpowers above the heads of those most affected (17:45, 17:50).

European leaders and US peace envoys insisted that some progress has been made in discussions on ending the Russian war of aggression in Ukraine, although they struck a cautious note about Putin’s intentions in the coming months (15:46, 18:38, 18:44).

US envoy Jared Kushner claimed that Russia’s leadership appears to be “comfortable” with the concept of Article 5-like security guarantees for Ukraine in any postwar settlement (18:29).

Meanwhile, Russia’s Putin struck an uncompromising tone at his press briefing in Shenzhen, vowing “painful” response to Ukraine’s attacks on Kerch bridge and defending his maximalist demands (13:09, 13:34).

If you have any tips, comments or suggestions, email me at jakub.krupa@theguardian.com.

I am also on Bluesky at @jakubkrupa.bsky.social and on X at @jakubkrupa.

Is Europe now in the shadow of a Trump, Putin and Xi alliance? – podcast

Andy Burnham is meeting western leaders in Berlin and Brussels this week, to discuss Ukraine and closer ties to the EU. Meanwhile, Donald Trump,Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping have met at the Apec summit in China.

Is this the start of a global shift of power away from Europe, or was it just a hyped-up photo opportunity?

Here is our latest “Politics Weekly” podcast on this if you want to catch up on today’s events:

Separately, Poland’s Donald Tusk also told reporters on his way back to Poland that Trump’s comments after his meeting with Putin and Xi sounded “quite optimistic.”

But Tusk quickly added that Trump’s “faith in Putin’s good will is probably unshakeable,” and he was a bit more sceptical about it.

“It would be good if indeed sooner or later it turned out that Russia is seriously ready to undertake peace talks,” he said.

But he warned:

“I don’t think it’s likely that Russia will sit down at the negotiating table in any serious way before the winter is over.”

'Some grounds for optimism' that talks can progress, Burnham says

The European leaders also get asked about Welt/Politico’s report earlier and the tone of Trump’s comments.

Burnham says that Trump’s comments focused on “horrific” loss of life during the war, saying “he spoke quite passionately about that subject.”

He stresses “nobody is winning this war,” and stresses that in his view there has been “huge progress” in now consensus that “there is no decision about Ukraine without Ukraine in the room and no decision about European security without Europe represented in the room.”

He says “there is a greater degree of alignment.”

“I would say for the first time in my period as prime minister of the United Kingdom, I see alignment; I see people saying the same thing; I see solidarity across the board in Europe; a strong, united European position.

And that gives some grounds for optimism that there can now be progress. But obviously, there is one person who can determine that more than anybody else, and that is president Putin.”

Witkoff jumps in there to say that Trump has “adamantly supported a peaceful end to this war,” with clear instructions to engage with the coalition of the willing and work in all formats that can be helpful to end the war.

“What I heard from him on the call today was that he mentioned these very same principles to the other two leaders who he was meeting with [Xi and Putin], so he made Ukraine, and a peaceful end to this war, a principal part of that trilateral today, and I think he’s to be commended for that.”

Russia 'comfortable' with Article 5-like security guarantees for Ukraine, Kushner says

Kushner says that the US managed to get Moscow comfortable with the concept that any security agreement for Ukraine would be based on Article 5-type arrangement, like in Nato.

(Not sure the Russians would say the same.)

He says “I know that there’s a lot of, scepticism and disbelief on that concept in Russia, but that’s why it’s important to restart the dialogue between Europe and Russia.”

He says:

“I will say from America’s perspective, giving an Article Five like security guarantee is a really, really big deal. And I think that that’s something that President Trump is open to. but obviously it has to be in America’s interest to do that and … we have to make sure it is part of a broader security package.”

Merz gets a question on potential multilateral talks with Ukraine, Russia, Europe and the US, and confirms that’s the plan and adds that finding the right place for it shouldn’t be too difficult.

He also goes back to his Yalta reference earlier, saying Europe was “parcelled up” by powers, and “we will not allow anything like that to happen again.”

Macron says the focus is on safeguarding Europe’s security.

He said that a peace declaration agreed by Donald Trump, Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping in China “does not lead to a reorganisation of the world”.

“Today, if there is one critical factor in Europe’s reorganisation, its security, it is precisely the meeting that took place in Berlin,” he said.

Trump comes away from China talks thinking peace is achievable, Kushner says

US Kushner is up next.

He says the meeting was “very substantive and successful,” and “essential in helping us shape our point of views,” as he confirms that Trump dialled in for parts of the talks.

He pointedly praises Italy’s Meloni, Poland’s Tusk, European Commission’s von der Leyen, Nato’s Rutte, Finnish president and Norwegian PMs, Stubb and Gahr Støre.

He says Europe is “very united, and very, very strong in their support of Ukraine,” which he and Witkoff “relayed to president Trump.”

He says, without revealing details, that Trump came away from the trilateral China meeting thinking “peace is achievable”.

“For us, success in an outcome would be to have a sovereign, secure, prosperous and free Ukraine at the end of the war,” he says.

He says the talks have been making “a lot of progress” on postwar prosperity plan, security guarantees, and a plan to exchange prisoners of war.

On postwar security, he says that “Nato will be a central pillar” of proposals, with the right structures to avoid accidental escalations.

Kushner also says that Russians appear to be “willing to trust” the US suggestion that Europeans need to be included in the process to make sure that whatever agreement is struck will be respected.

The US envoys will be meeting with national security advisers next to agree on the detail of their proposals.

“President Trump wants to make a deal with Europe by his side,” he insists..

“Our goal is really to end this war and to really help build a durable peace. We are very committed. President Trump, will do whatever it takes to do that. He’s instructed us to commit as much time as possible, and we will continue to do that in full coordination, and unity with our European partners.”

'Not for the aggressor to set out wide raging and unrealistic security demands' Burnham says

UK’s Burnham speaks next.

He says today’s meeting “has put on a huge show of support” for Kyiv, and “the mood was stronger, more united, more determined.”

“Europe has a clear and consistent and united negotiating position. It’s not for the aggressor in this conflict to set out wide ranging and unrealistic security demands. That much we are all absolutely clear about.”

He says the coalition is ready for discussions on European security, but only “if there is a peace agreement between Ukraine and Russia.”

He says the UK’s support for Ukraine will continue for “as long as it takes.”

“Europe has a clear and consistent and united negotiating position. It’s not for the aggressor in this conflict to set out wide ranging and unrealistic security demands. That much we are all absolutely clear about.

And I hope that message is heard very clearly, in Moscow: for as long as it takes.”

“If we want to be credible in peace negotiations, then it is important that Ukraine defends itself and goes into these negotiations in a good position, and Ukraine can only do so if we continue supporting Ukraine.”

He adds:

“Everyone who is here today have to do everything in their power so that Ukraine has everything it needs in order to resist and to defend herself …”

He says that faced with Russia’s maximalist demands, it’s time it is “the right point in time to discuss [Ukraine’s] Nato membership.”

Commenting on the current state of talks, he says Russia “did not submit any concrete and tangible proposals for peace.”

He acknowledges that “the coming weeks will be critical” for Ukraine, and so the coalition gathered at the right moment.

He says there was every attempt made to “make this meeting as concrete as possible.”

He thanks all partners for helping Ukraine and highlights “active efforts to ensure that we stand firm.”

He thanks the EU for its “very substantial” proposed loan of £45bn.

He also highlights some of the priority areas for Ukraine, including the move to stop daily drone attacks (which he confirms hit the Austrian and the Dutch embassies), and deploy more air defence systems.

He also says the next round of talks should include European leaders, and highlights the importance of security guarantees and Ukraine’s future membership in the EU.

articles.body:
Xi-Trump-Putin summit: What did it achieve?

November 19, 2026

The presidents of China, the US and Russia have held an unprecedented summit. While Trump said the three leaders were "making history," Xi described the talks as "fruitful" and Putin called them "open and candid."

Chinese President Xi Jinping hosted US President Donald Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin on Thursday for an unprecedented trilateral summit in Shenzhen, bringing together the leaders of the world's three most powerful military powers amid heightened geopolitical tensions.

Xi hailed the talks as "groundbreaking," saying discussions ranged from global governance and denuclearization to the war in Ukraine and energy security.

The "peace declaration" released after their meeting made no mention of Russia's war in Ukraine or the US-led war in Iran.

Instead, the three leaders agreed to pursue reforms of the United Nations, limit the role of the International Criminal Court and reaffirm their commitment to avoiding nuclear war. They also pledged to boost supplies of refined petroleum products to address global energy challenges.

The tightly choreographed meeting fueled concerns that Beijing, Washington and Moscow could seek to reshape the international order around competing spheres of influence.

While Xi said the talks with Trump and Putin were "positive, constructive and fruitful," Trump heralded the gathering as "really making history."

Who gained the most from the meeting?

For Putin, the three-way talks, and his meetings with both leaders separately earlier, offered a chance to show the world that he was on par with the leaders of the US and China, despite Western efforts to isolate him since he launched the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.

Emma Chanlett-Avery, senior director for Political-Security Affairs at the Asia Society Policy Institute (ASPI), said Putin had the most to gain from the meeting as "he appeared on the world stage as one of the dominant players in the world."

Chim Lee, a senior analyst with The Economist Intelligence Unit (EIU), echoed this view.

The meeting itself is a "major outcome for Russia," he told DW, pointing to Russian media coverage that has cast it as "reinforcing Russia's standing in the world."

Beijing reluctant to accept nuclear limits

The joint statement also said the leaders are committed to work to reduce nuclear risks and prevent nuclear proliferation.

The last nuclear arms pact between Russia and the United States, known as New START, expired in February.

Trump has said he wants "a new, improved and modernized" deal that includes China.

But Beijing has so far been reluctant to accept limits as its estimated arsenal of around 500 warheads remains far smaller than those of Russia and the US.

Moscow and Washington are believed to possess more than 5,000 warheads each.

Lee said China is unlikely to participate in a trilateral institutionalized setting to control nuclear arms.

"The gap between China's nuclear arsenal and those of Russia and US is still quite large. From China's perspective, it doesn't seem to make a lot of sense to put the three powers in the same bucket in this area."

The expert believes Trump attended the meeting as he is "actively thinking about his legacy in the final two years in office."

"So, in this context, the idea of setting up a trilateral nuclear arms control arrangement would have been a very big achievement," Lee said.

But, in the end, the declaration said the countries would merely engage in "dialogue" on the issue, avoiding any explicit commitments to downsize their nuclear stockpiles.

A reluctant host?

China initially hesitated to organize the trilateral summit as it did not want to be explicitly tied to Russia's war in Ukraine and harm Beijing's efforts to present itself as a long-term force for global stability.

The Chinese government, which is working to rebalance economic ties with the EU, was also wary of appearing to form a G3 club with Washington and Moscow, which could alienate other global partners.

Chanlett-Avery said that China had some degree of discomfort in convening this meeting, worried about getting involved in Ukraine issues.

But Beijing eventually "managed to get the outcome they wanted" and kept the European conflict out of the meeting's focus, she noted.

"China was able to show off Shenzhen and all of its sparkling high-tech features. They convened a successful international meeting that grabbed lots of headlines," she added. "So, I think China probably came out feeling okay."

Warnings of a 'second Yalta'

Prior to the summit, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy had warned of a "second Yalta," referring to the Yalta Conference held in Crimea in 1945.

That meeting saw the Allied powers decide on the post-war European order following the end of World War II.

In Shenzhen, Putin stressed that Russia, the US and China, as victors in World War II and veto-wielding members of the UN Security Council, bore a "joint responsibility for maintaining international peace."

But Ying-Yu Lin, Associate Professor at Graduate Institute of International Affairs and Strategic Studies at Taiwan's Tamkang University, said the Yalta comparison "is a bit of a stretch," given the vast differences between 1945 and now.

Will there be more such trilaterals?

Putin also said that all three leaders "agree that it's a useful format," and such meetings could take place again.

Lee, the EIU expert, said the trilateral setup "is unlikely to be just a one-off" and there will probably be more such meetings in the coming years.

"Especially from the US side to have this kind of setup, there will be some interest in maintaining warm relations with both China and Russia," he underlined.

articles.title: Houthis hit Saudi Arabia's sovereign wealth fund skyscraper
articles.summary: Houthis hit Saudi Arabia's sovereign wealth fund skyscraper The skyscraper housing Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund (PIF) in Riyadh was damaged on Thursday by a Houthi strike, the kingdom has confirmed. The strike destroyed windows across seven to eight floors of the tower, Riyadh's tallest skyscraper, and bent part of its metal facade, according to a Reuters journalist. Video footage shared from the Saudi capital showed crews already working to replace the glass. The attack is the second time this month that the Houthis have struck at the heart of Saudi Arabia’s image as a safe investment destination. PIF says it has around $1 trillion in assets. Earlier this month, the Houthis struck Aramco Tower in Riyadh. “One of the towers of the Financial Center in Riyadh was targeted in a terrorist attack by the terrorist Houthi militia, causing material damage but no injuries -praise be to God,” the Saudi authorities said in a statement released on Thursday. The press release included an image showing notable but relatively minor damage to the PIF headquarters. Video footage appeared to show a missile slamming into the 80-storey tower, but Middle East Eye could not independently verify the footage. r

articles.body:
Long before Dario Amodei butted heads with the Pentagon over whether the U.S. military could use Anthropic’s models for mass domestic surveillance and fully autonomous weapons, he was fighting another battle.

At the California Institute of Technology in 2003, Amodei called on his classmates to join him in protesting the U.S. invasion of Iraq, writing in an op-ed that citizen-scientists should not be “reduced to amoral technicians who run the machines of war.”

On Thursday, as 43-year-old Amodei led his startup to an initial public offering that raised a record $81 billion and valued it at about $1.5 trillion, the listing cemented his transformation from an idealistic physics student into one of the most powerful custodians of the artificial intelligence age.

articles.title: Europe ready for talks with Russia on ending war in Ukraine, leaders say
articles.summary: European allies of Ukraine say they have a "united" negotiating position at a summit in Berlin.
articles.preview: European leaders have said they are ready for negotiations with Russia on ending the war in Ukraine, in a strong show of support for Kyiv. "Europe has a clear and consistent and united negotiating position," UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham said, while German Chancellor Friedrich Merz stressed that Moscow's "maximalist demands are not realistic". They were speaking at Berlin's summit of Ukraine's allies known as the Coalition of the Willing.
articles.body:
European leaders have said they are ready for negotiations with Russia on ending the war in Ukraine, in a strong show of support for Kyiv.

"Europe has a clear and consistent and united negotiating position," UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham said, while German Chancellor Friedrich Merz stressed that Moscow's "maximalist demands are not realistic".

They were speaking at Berlin's summit of Ukraine's allies known as the Coalition of the Willing.

Donald Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner, one of the two US envoys who were in Berlin, said the US president wanted to make a deal with Moscow "with Europe by his side". Russia's Vladimir Putin has so far rejected any European role in the US-led peace talks.

Trump had earlier held historic trilateral talks in Shenzhen, south-eastern China, with Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping and later dialled into the Berlin summit from Air Force One.

In a lengthy press conference following his talks with Trump and Xi, Putin addressed the question of multilateral peace talks, saying the Americans were "insistently" asking Russia to allow the Europeans to take part.

Putin claimed Russia was not against the idea but said Moscow wanted to clarify "what Europe will bring to these talks".

"That is why, through diplomatic channels, we have invited the Europeans to come to Moscow in order to determine their positions. And after that, we will decide in what format we will continue the dialogue with Ukraine."

But Putin also said that "every day" Russia heard that European leaders were talking about war coming in 2030. "But we are not planning to attack anyone... Is that normal? I do not think so," he said. Still, Putin added, Russia understood that "discussing issues linked to security in Europe is pointless without the Europeans".

Jared Kushner told reporters that the US president had come away from Shenzhen believing that "peace is achievable".

Striking an upbeat note, Kushner said that the Russians were willing to trust the instinct of the US envoys "on our behalf" that the Europeans should be at the table and that Moscow was now "comfortable" with Ukraine having security guarantees based on the idea enshrined in Nato's Article Five that requires allies to come to a country's defence if it comes under attack.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, who also was at the summit in Germany's capital, has long sought a guarantee equivalent to Nato's collective defence clause, and there has been little indication that Putin would accept that kind of condition.

Russia rejects outright the idea of Ukrainian membership of Nato, but reports say US negotiators have mulled the idea of giving Kyiv Article Five-style guarantees without being part of the Western defensive alliance if it agrees to painful territorial concessions.

Zelensky and the three European leaders â Merz, Burnham and French President Emmanuel Macron â were not as upbeat as Kushner, and the Ukrainian president made clear that the Russian president had spurned every proposal so far: "Putin has always said no."

The German chancellor was equally sceptical, although he said with US involvement the chance of peace was increasing. Europe was willing to enter "serious discussions on European security" with Russia, he explained, "as long as it's matched with a serious discussion and only first a peace agreement with Ukraine".

"These talks have to begin, and we will accept if conditions are acceptable for Europe and Ukraine," said Merz.

He also said any attempts to divide Europe into spheres of influence run by major powers was unacceptable, amid concerns on the continent that this issue may have been on the agenda at the trilateral talks in Shenzhen.

- Analysis: Trilateral summit high on spectacle, short on substance

- Published9 hours ago

"A 'Yalta format' will not bring peace," Merz said, referring to the post-World War Two agreement between the US, the USSR and Britain in 1945.

He also sought to downplay the Shenzhen summit as above all "a photo opportunity."

"The US understands that there can be no peace without us. We, in turn, know that with the United States by our side, the prospects for peace increase," Merz added.

Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk also took exception to Trump's description of Putin as a "friend" at the Shenzhen summit, saying: "Mr Putin is not our friend and will never be."

Meanwhile, Macron urged Ukraine's allies to do the "maximum" to deliver the much-needed air defence systems Kyiv needed to repel deadly Russian attacks.

The French leader also urged the allies to "reopen the question" of Ukraine's membership in Nato.

There have been mixed messages from Moscow on European participation to the talks. Last week, following a visit to Moscow, the US envoys, Steve Witkoff and Kushner, appeared certain that Europe would soon have a seat at the negotiating table.

But the Russians were more circumspect and this week Putin's aide Yury Ushakov said a "great deal" would have to be done before the format could be expanded, suggesting that several more rounds of discussions would have to be held before any four-sided talks could take place.

Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.

While Russia has engaged with several rounds of talks over the last year, little in Moscow's rhetoric or actions suggests that the Kremlin is considering scaling down its war on Ukraine.

It continues to pound Kyiv's energy infrastructure to cripple it as winter takes hold, increasing numbers of civilian casualties are being recorded across the country, and Kremlin officials have not budged from Russia's demands for Ukrainian sovereign territory.

As delegations were meeting in China and Germany on Thursday, several buildings in Kyiv's historic centre came under attack from drones. One person was killed in a strike on a residential building in the Podilskyi neighbourhood, while the Dutch and Austrian embassies as well as Saint Volodymyr's Cathedral reported damage.

And Putin also vowed that Moscow's response to a Ukrainian strike on the Crimean Bridge linking Russia with occupied Crimea would be "considerably more painful" than what Kyiv had achieved.

He also said he had discussed a "possible ceasefire in a number of areas" but had decided against it after the attack on the bridge.

Still, Putin claimed to be "interested" in ending the war and was ready to make compromises, while Ukraine and Europe were not.

"I assure you, we have no desire at all to continue this armed conflict," Putin said, despite the fact that Russia has in recent months intensified its attacks on Ukraine's critical infrastructure as cold winter approaches.

Kyiv and its European allies say that â in the absence of any major success on the vast front line â the Kremlin leader is seeking to break Ukrainian resistance by leaving millions of civilians without electricity and water supply.

articles.title: Commentary: As Southeast Asia cracks down on scammers, a new base emerges
articles.summary: The detention of 130 Malaysians in a Pakistan scam centre raid shows why efforts to combat scam syndicates must extend beyond Southeast Asia, says former foreign correspondent Nirmal Ghosh.
articles.preview: The detention of 130 Malaysians in a Pakistan scam centre raid shows why efforts to combat scam syndicates must extend beyond Southeast Asia, says former foreign correspondent Nirmal Ghosh. SINGAPORE: Under pressure from crackdowns since 2025, the model of large, centralised scam compounds in Southeast Asia is evolving. Some syndicates are shifting into smaller decentralised units and finding bases in countries with relatively weaker enforcement. Countries in South Asia like Pakistan and Sri Lanka are now scrambling to respond.
articles.body:
The detention of 130 Malaysians in a Pakistan scam centre raid shows why efforts to combat scam syndicates must extend beyond Southeast Asia, says former foreign correspondent Nirmal Ghosh.

SINGAPORE: Under pressure from crackdowns since 2025, the model of large, centralised scam compounds in Southeast Asia is evolving. Some syndicates are shifting into smaller decentralised units and finding bases in countries with relatively weaker enforcement.

Countries in South Asia like Pakistan and Sri Lanka are now scrambling to respond.

NEW BASES IN SOUTH ASIA

One early alternative for the scam syndicates was Sri Lanka, due to relatively easy entry visa rules, accessible and reliable high-speed internet, and affordable cost of living including rentals, with apartments and villas becoming preferred bases. Since the start of 2026, Sri Lankan police have arrested over 1,100 foreign nationals, mostly from China, Vietnam and India, for alleged involvement in cybercrime. Officials said the networks were targeting people across Asia.

Pakistan is also on the map. A raid on a suspected scam centre in Rawalpindi in October, in which 130 Malaysians were detained, provided the “smoking gun”, a local expert on organised crime told me.

The Malaysians – some on valid and some on expired visas according to Malaysian authorities – were arrested in a relatively high-end mixed-use apartment and office building on the southern outskirts of Rawalpindi. They had reportedly been posing as bank and police officers targeting Malaysians, informing them of suspicious transactions and pressuring them into transferring money.

Pakistani media reported that the operation was believed to be run by a Malaysian based in Cambodia, with supervisors in Pakistan. Malaysian police last week said a team was being sent to Pakistan to assist in the investigation. The Pakistani expert who spoke to me called it a “franchise displacement model”.

Earlier in August, Pakistani authorities raided an alleged scam centre in Islamabad’s affluent Gulberg Green neighbourhood, detaining 258 foreigners, including 40 Chinese and 170 from Vietnam. Authorities said they had arrived on tourist visas.

Pakistan had relatively easy visa-on-arrival rules until early 2026, cheap office space, a large English-speaking youth pool, and gaps in oversight. The 2025 Sumsub Global Fraud Index which measures exposure and lack of digital safeguards, listed it as the most vulnerable to digital fraud among 112 countries included.

KEEPING PACE WITH SCAMMERS

The spread into South Asia is testing the ability of governments to keep pace.

Pakistan has been trying to gear up. After a slow start, a full-fledged independent authority, the National Cyber Crime Investigation Agency, became operational last year. There is also ongoing debate over whether Pakistani provinces should have their own independent provincial versions of this agency.

On Monday (Nov 16) the US Embassy in Colombo in a statement said an FBI team would be spending a week in Sri Lanka this month training local investigators and helping to identify victims, trace criminal activity, and build stronger cases against online scammers.

India has also been stepping up efforts. Its Supreme Court on Oct 29 ordered WhatsApp and other online platforms to inform it of measures to prevent “digital arrest” scams - in which scammers pose as police officers, intimidating their targets. The court also pressed for rules requiring financial institutions to cover a victim’s entire loss when their failure to take reasonable precautions caused the fraud.

In December 2025, India’s Central Bureau of Investigation, acting on information from the US’ FBI, arrested six alleged leaders of syndicates targeting Americans. This year has seen dozens of scam and financial fraud operations broken up, with thousands of arrests.

BORDERLESS CRIME CALLS FOR BORDERLESS RESPONSE

Given the scam industry’s ability to adapt, efforts need to widen to reflect the global reach of the criminal syndicates.

“South Asia stands out as a region most significantly affected by trafficking in persons for forced criminality into Southeast Asia, but it is also an emerging operational hub,” says a September 2026 briefing note by the Global Initiative Against Transnational Organised Crime (GITOC).

It also highlights convergence between cyber scam operations in Southeast Asia and South Asia-based recruitment and trafficking networks, and criminal organisations in South Asia involved in job and visitor visa scams.

The dispersal of scam syndicates to South Asia underscores their fluid nature, which seeks the weakest and most vulnerable jurisdictions. Scam syndicates and associated criminality, including human trafficking and money laundering, do not recognise state borders. They are enabled by a borderless digital world and increasingly optimised by AI.

For regulatory and enforcement authorities to keep pace the response to transnational crime should be equally borderless, with enhanced information sharing between agencies across South and Southeast Asia.

That Malaysian and Pakistani police are jointly investigating the Rawalpindi case, and that the FBI is training Sri Lankan investigators, is encouraging. Such joint efforts need to be enhanced within the region as well to deal with this complex and predatory criminal industry.

Nirmal Ghosh, a former foreign correspondent, is an author and independent writer based in Singapore. He is also on the Board of GI-TOC, but this piece is written in his personal capacity. He writes a monthly column for CNA, published every third Friday.

articles.body:
Zimbabwe

The HALO Trust, the world's largest landmine clearance charity, reports that it has destroyed 250,000 landmines in Zimbabwe since 2013. This accomplishment marks a significant milestone in efforts to eliminate explosives left over from the liberation war of the 1970s.

The organization said its Zimbabwean teams have spent the past 13 years clearing minefields in the districts of Rushinga and Mount Darwin, helping restore farmland, reconnect communities and improve access to services. "We are super excited because again, it means a lot of things.

One, we're talking about peace of mind. Just that. It's one of the things that people often overlook, but then just knowing that this threat is gone and it is gone forever is just one of the biggest impacts of the work that we do of this mine being destroyed," said Nokutenda Masiyanise, Head of Donor Management and Partnerships at HALO Zimbabwe.

In Rushinga, HALO said clearance operations have benefited more than 14,000 residents by allowing families to graze livestock safely, cultivate crops, and access schools, clinics, markets, and water sources.

HALO, Zimbabwe’s largest demining operator, also employs local residents, including female deminers who often support large extended families.

The charity said it is using drones, advanced detectors and small excavators to speed up clearance efforts but warned that international aid cuts could jeopardize Zimbabwe’s goal of becoming mine-free by 2030.

articles.title: Dl scuola, gli e-book spaccano la maggioranza. FI vota contro, poi l'emendamento passa in Senato
articles.summary: AGI - L'avvertimento era arrivato ieri: Forza Italia è contraria alla norma sugli e-book . Ma FdI ha tenuto il punto sull'emendamento che stabilisce per gli editori l'obbligo di vendere la versione digitale dei libri scolastici e universitari a un prezzo inferiore di almeno il 50% rispetto alle edizioni cartacee. E così la maggioranza al Senato si spacca, con gli azzurri che votano contro e Azione che si aggiunge ai voti favorevoli delle altre forze di centrodestra. L'emendamento passa in Aula L'emendamento, presentato al Decreto Scuola, che tra le altre norme introduce il tetto del 30% di alunni stranieri con insufficiente conoscenza dell'italiano nelle classi, viene prima bocciato in Commissione Bilancio, sempre con i voti contrari di Forza Italia. Poi, messo in votazione in Aula, passa per 8 voti di differenza (84 sì e 76 no), con il via libera di FdI, presenti in massa, Lega e Noi Moderati, a cui si aggiungono i voti dei calendiani. Contrarie tutte le altre forze di opposizione, che protestano in Aula con cartelli e slogan. Il decreto, alla fine, viene approvato con i sì di tutto il centrodestra (80 voti favorevoli e 46 contrari) e trasmesso alla Camera per il via libera definitivo. Il peso delle assenze e il passaggio alla Camera 'Pesano' le assenze tra le fila delle opposizioni, che avrebbero potuto ribaltare l'esito del voto. Intanto nella maggioranza si guarda già all'iter a Montecitorio. Il decreto va convertito in legge entro il 29 novembre. Fonti parlamentari azzurre spiegano che alla Camera FI potrebbe presentare un proprio emendamento sul tema degli e-book, mentre non viene escluso che il governo possa porre la questione di fiducia, visti anche i tempi ristretti per l'esame. Le opposizioni all'attacco Al di là di quanto accadrà nel passaggio a Montecitorio, le opposizioni ne approfittano per evidenziare le divisioni del centrodestra. "C'è un dato politico che non state considerando, Forza Italia ha dato la sfiducia al governo sulla scuola, su questo voto finisce la legislatura, se avete un briciolo di dignità riportate il Paese al voto", sentenzia il leader di Iv Matteo Renzi. "Il fatto politico della giornata è che mi sembra non ci sia più una maggioranza", incalza la segretaria del Pd Elly Schlein. Anche per M5s "la maggioranza è a pezzi. Hanno votato contro il loro stesso emendamento, è un nodo politico enorme. Non si sono dimessi dopo il referendum e dopo essersi spaccati sulla legge elettorale, non lo faranno nemmeno stavolta. Ma almeno prendano atto del fatto che sono in tilt e ritirino questa decreto", afferma il capogruppo Luca Pirondini. E Avs aggiunge: "C'è una spaccatura evidente dentro la maggioranza e diamo la parola agli elettori", chiosa Peppe De Cristofaro La replica di Forza Italia FI nega la spaccatura e minimizza la portata del voto: si tratta solo di un emendamento. "Non c'entra niente la tenuta della maggioranza, non c'entra niente il governo", tiene a puntualizzare il leader azzurro e vicepremier Antonio Tajani, che fa sapere di aver "avvisato in anticipo che avremmo votato contro, lo sapevano tutti. Lo sapeva la premier, erano tutti informati". E la capogruppo Stefania Craxi assicura: "Da Forza Italia non c'è stata nessuna sfida a nessuno e non c'è nessuna rottura della maggioranza". La posizione di Fratelli d'Italia Anche in FdI si preferisce non dare alcuna enfasi al voto odierno, rispedendo al mittente le accuse delle opposizioni. Non c'è nessuna crisi di governo, è la linea. Per di più, viene ricordato, il governo non è coinvolto, trattandosi di un emendamento parlamentare sul quale l'esecutivo stesso si è rimesso all'Aula. Certo, il no di FI non viene accolto con favore, ma non sorprende. Semmai, è sempre il ragionamento, è l'opposizione a uscirne male, non essendo riuscita a incassare una vittoria nonostante la non compattezza della maggioranza. Insomma, nessun casus belli e, soprattutto, nessuna conseguenza sulla tenuta di governo e maggioranza, spiegano fonti di FdI che, comunque, tengono a ribadire: la norma resta e verrà confermata alla Camera, nessun passo indietro . Centrosinistra e Italia Viva insistono sulla frattura Il centrosinistra non ha intenzione di mollare la presa e insiste sulla frattura che si è consumata al Senato. "Forza Italia ha votato con tutte le opposizioni dapprima in Commissione, affossando il provvedimento sugli e-book", dice il vicepresidente Iv Enrico Borghi, e "di fronte a questo risultato, Fratelli d'Italia ha sfidato il partito di Marina e Piersilvio Berlusconi, e ha ripresentato l'emendamento per l'Aula mandando il sottosegretario Fazzolari a fare da guardiano dei suoi e sfidando Forza Italia", afferma. La presenza di Fazzolari in Aula, sia nella giornata di ieri che oggi, viene rimarcata anche dal capogruppo Pd Francesco Boccia: "Sembra essere il dominus di questo decreto visto che pontifica attraverso i mezzi d'informazione e dà anche consigli alle opposizioni". Botta e risposta finale tra Schlein e Calenda A fine giornata arriva il botta e risposta tra Schlein e Calenda. La leader dem confessa: "Certo che mi preoccupa" che Azione abbia votato con la destra, "spero non sia una scelta definitiva". Replica il leader di Azione: "E Schlein vota con le case editrici contro un taglio del 50% del costo dei libri per i ragazzi. Spero sia un caso perché altrimenti ci troveremmo davanti a una progressista che guarda al progresso delle case editrici e non al fatto che i giovani italiani possano pagare meno i libri per studiare".

articles.title: Meloni: "Non può esserci pace in Ucraina senza l'Europa"
articles.summary: AGI - "A Dublino, noi leader abbiamo stabilito come accompagnare questo processo: un team europeo", nel cosiddetto formato E5, nel quale è presente l'Italia, "che lavora in stretta collaborazione con l'Ucraina e gli Stati Uniti. Ora dobbiamo conferire a questo team un mandato chiaro: cosa chiediamo, cosa offriamo e cosa non accetteremo mai". Così la presidente del Consiglio, Giorgia Meloni, si è rivolta ai partecipanti al vertice dei Volenterosi per l'Ucraina a Berlino. "E non ci presentiamo a mani vuote", ha sottolineato ancora la premier, "questa coalizione sta lavorando a garanzie di sicurezza, incluso l'impegno ispirato all'Articolo 5 proposto dall'Italia - un modello che ora si trova sul tavolo negoziale". Tuttavia, nel testo non si fa menzione della guerra in Ucraina. Ciò ci suggerisce due cose. Lo scambio di prigionieri concordato ad Abu Dhabi è un segnale positivo; accogliamo con favore ogni passo di natura umanitaria. Ma la vera prova consiste nell'interruzione verificabile degli attacchi alle infrastrutture energetiche". "A Shenzhen, i tre leader hanno ribadito l'importanza di flussi energetici stabili. Bene. Prendiamoli in parola, a cominciare dalla rete elettrica ucraina. È una questione che ci riguarda tutti: la sicurezza delle centrali nucleari nel nostro continente, milioni di civili che affrontano l'inverno, mercati energetici già sotto pressione. Non soltanto sul piano economico, ma anche attraverso un'agenda politica e negoziale definita, sulla quale si continuerà a lavorare a livello di consiglieri, insieme agli inviati speciali americani e ucraini. Il siparietto con Merz e il colloquio con Kushner Meloni ha lasciato il summit al termine dei lavori per volare a Roma e collegarsi con gli altri leader di centrodestra per fare il punto sulla manovra. Al suo arrivo in Cancelleria, dove si è svolto il summit, la premier è stata protagonista di un simpatico siparietto: l'auto su cui viaggiava non si è fermata davanti al tappeto rosso allestito dal cerimoniale, ma solo qualche metro più avanti, e ha dovuto fare una breve retromarcia. "Giorgia, vai troppo veloce", ha scherzato Merz prima di abbracciarla e stringerle la mano. A margine della foto di famiglia, la premier ha avuto anche un breve colloquio con Jared Kushner, uno dei due inviati Usa per l'Ucraina, nonché genero di Trump.
