articles.title: Il principe Harry: 'Mi riarruolerei per combattere contro la Russia'
articles.summary: Al Telegraph: 'Gb in conflitto con Mosca ormai da un decennio'
articles.preview: Il principe Harry è pronto a rimettere la divisa, se il Regno Unito dovesse averne bisogno di fronte alla "minaccia" della Russia. A undici anni dal congedo, il duca di Sussex si è detto disposto a riarruolarsi nelle Forze armate britanniche in un'intervista esclusiva al podcast del Telegraph 'Ukraine: The Latest', registrata a Leopoli durante la sua visita a sorpresa in Ucraina dello scorso fine settimana.
articles.body:
Il principe Harry è pronto a rimettere la divisa, se il Regno Unito dovesse averne bisogno di fronte alla "minaccia" della Russia. A undici anni dal congedo, il duca di Sussex si è detto disposto a riarruolarsi nelle Forze armate britanniche in un'intervista esclusiva al podcast del Telegraph 'Ukraine: The Latest', registrata a Leopoli durante la sua visita a sorpresa in Ucraina dello scorso fine settimana.

"Se mi venisse chiesto di arruolarmi nuovamente, qualora ce ne fosse bisogno, sarei disponibile al 100% per servire il mio Paese al fianco dei miei commilitoni reduci e del personale militare in servizio", ha dichiarato il secondogenito di re Carlo III. Durante la visita, la quarta dall'inizio della guerra con la Russia, Harry aveva assistito alle selezioni della squadra ucraina per gli Invictus Games, da lui creati, promettendo ai militari feriti di sostenere Kiev nell'organizzazione dell'evento quando "l'Ucraina avrà vinto".

Il principe si è riferito nello specifico alla situazione del Paese invaso, per cui già in passato non ha nascosto un forte supporto, sostenendo che "c'è molto da imparare". E ha aggiunto che, a suo parere, anche il Regno Unito in realtà è in conflitto con Mosca ormai da un decennio. "Solo perché non ci sono droni, proiettili e razzi che ci volano addosso, non significa che non siamo in guerra", è la sua considerazione.

Secondo Harry, "l'Europa ha preso coscienza della minaccia" rappresentata dalla Russia, ma il suo "maggiore timore" è che il continente possa "dividersi". Interpellato sulla situazione geopolitica attuale, ha risposto: "Penso che dovremmo essere tutti preoccupati, assolutamente. E penso che dovremmo essere preparati e che coloro tra noi che hanno prestato servizio dovrebbero essere pronti a farlo nuovamente". Il principe ha esortato a "raddoppiare il nostro sostegno" per Kiev invece di fare un passo indietro, pur osservando che "serve una qualche forma di strategia d'uscita per la Russia".

Senza nominare Donald Trump, ha inoltre criticato l'approccio della Casa Bianca, sottolineando la "grande separazione" tra il sostegno all'Ucraina della società americana e la linea di "un'amministrazione" che "forse la pensava diversamente". Harry aveva già prestato servizio nell'esercito per circa dieci anni, completando due turni in Afghanistan, il secondo dei quali come pilota di elicotteri Apache, prima del congedo arrivato nel 2015.

articles.title: Nearly a quarter of the world’s children live in conflict zones, according to Save the Children
articles.summary: A 'record rate' of 589 million children were living in war zones in 2025, with 44% of them in Africa.
articles.preview: Nearly a quarter of the world's children are currently living in a conflict zone, a record rate since statistics were first recorded in the 1990s, the charity Save the Children said on Thursday, November 19. "Almost one in four children worldwide are now living in conflict zones, the highest number since records began in 1990," the London-based charity said. "The figure represents an increase of more than 50% in a decade, jumping from 378 million in 2015 to 589 million in 2025," it added.
articles.body:
Nearly a quarter of the world's children are currently living in a conflict zone, a record rate since statistics were first recorded in the 1990s, the charity Save the Children said on Thursday, November 19.

"Almost one in four children worldwide are now living in conflict zones, the highest number since records began in 1990," the London-based charity said. "The figure represents an increase of more than 50% in a decade, jumping from 378 million in 2015 to 589 million in 2025," it added.

The report was titled "Stop the War on Children: Changing the Odds" and drew on statistics from the Peace Research Institute Oslo (PRIO). The percentage of children living in conflict zones has doubled from 10% in the mid-1990s to 23.4% in 2025.

"These record-high figures are a stark reminder that conflict is devastating the daily lives, education, health and future prospects of hundreds of millions of children," said Gudrun Ostby, a research professor at PRIO. "Unless greater efforts are made to protect children in conflict settings, the consequences of today's wars will be felt for decades to come," he added.

The report defines conflict zones as areas existing within a 50-kilometer radius in which at least one armed attack took place. Africa has the largest number of children living in conflict zones, at about 260 million, or 44% of the total across the globe, the report found.

Rates have surged in the Middle East as well, from 52 million children in 2024 to 67 million in 2025, a 29% increase. An average of two in five children in Africa and the Middle East are living in conflict zones, it added.

"The scale of this crisis is rapidly growing, and the systems meant to protect children are being pushed to breaking point," said Inger Ashing, chief executive of Save The Children International.

articles.title: Israeli military completes ground operation in Gaza beyond Yellow Line
articles.summary: Hamas condemned the incursion, which the Israeli military said was to dismantle a "terror tunnel", as a "flagrant" ceasefire violation.
articles.preview: Israeli forces have completed a rare ground operation in part of central Gaza outside their control, the military says, a day after residents were ordered to evacuate. Families fled their homes and tents on Wednesday as tanks advanced into an area east of Nuseirat refugee camp and onto the territory's main north-south road under the cover of artillery strikes. The Israeli military said the "targeted" operation aimed to dismantle a "terror tunnel" west of the so-called Yellow Line, which marks the more than 60% of Gaza's territory occupied by Israel.
articles.body:
Israeli forces have completed a rare ground operation in part of central Gaza outside their control, the military says, a day after residents were ordered to evacuate.

Families fled their homes and tents on Wednesday as tanks advanced into an area east of Nuseirat refugee camp and onto the territory's main north-south road under the cover of artillery strikes.

The Israeli military said the "targeted" operation aimed to dismantle a "terror tunnel" west of the so-called Yellow Line, which marks the more than 60% of Gaza's territory occupied by Israel.

The Palestinian armed group Hamas, which controls the rest of Gaza, accused Israel of a "flagrant violation" of the October 2025 ceasefire deal.

Violence has continued in Gaza over the past 13 months, with near-daily Israeli strikes, and living conditions for the 2.1 million people there remain dire.

Wednesday's Israeli incursion deep beyond the Yellow Line was reportedly the first to be publicly announced by the Israel Defense Forces (IDF) since the ceasefire began.

In the early afternoon, Israeli military body Cogat's Arabic spokesperson announced the start of the operation and warned Palestinians living in an area north of Nuseirat and Bureij refugee camp to stay away for their own safety. It also said a section of Salah al-Din road that passed through the area would be closed to traffic.

In the evening, the IDF said the joint operation with the Shin Bet security service sought "to dismantle a terror tunnel west of the Yellow Line that posed an immediate and direct threat to IDF troops".

On Thursday morning, Cogat told Palestinians on social media that "the activity has ended, and the Salah al-Din axis has been reopened".

Hamas warned in a statement that the advance of Israeli military vehicles beyond the Yellow Line and the evacuation of residents constituted "a dangerous development and a flagrant violation of the ceasefire agreement".

Gaza's Hamas-run government media office meanwhile said that an estimated 6,000 people had fled their homes and tents because of the operation, and that this amounted to the war crime of forced displacement.

Footage published by Palestinian media outlets and on social media showed dozens of families fleeing areas near Nuseirat camp following the Israeli evacuation order.

In one video verified by BBC Verify, a man could be seen ducking after hearing artillery fire and then running along Salah al-Din road, about 1.5km (0.9 miles) west of the Yellow Line. "The Israeli occupation now is firing randomly near the houses and tents of people," he said.

An image, meanwhile, showed six armoured vehicles, including tanks and bulldozers, around Salah al-Din road.

A resident of Nuseirat who was forced to flee told BBC Arabic's Middle East Daily programme: "The situation is now extremely dire, with Israeli forces firing indiscriminately at areas where displaced people have sought shelter."

"We couldn't take any of our belongings with us - not even our blankets, pillows, or clothes. We had no choice but to leave everything behind."

A second resident also reported "indiscriminate gunfire and shelling" and said there had been "numerous casualties, including fatalities".

Asked about those reports, the IDF sent a general statement about the operation.

Multiple verified videos of the aftermath of the incursion on Thursday showed destruction, earth banks, and heavy vehicle tracks more than 1.2km beyond the Yellow Line.

That is believed to be the furthest Israeli troops have advanced into central Gaza since they occupied the so-called Netzarim Corridor before the ceasefire.

Some residents returned to check their properties following the Israeli withdrawal.

"The entire area has been destroyed, and we honestly do not know what to do," Abd Aliwa told Reuters news agency as he sat beside a pile of rubble.

- Israel moves Yellow Line deeper into Gaza, satellite images show

- Published16 January

Gaza's Hamas-run Civil Defence agency said three people were killed and others were wounded in three separate Israeli drone strikes on Wednesday.

One man was killed in Nuseirat, the second was killed to the north in Gaza City, and the third was killed in the central town of Deir al-Balah, it added.

The IDF told the BBC that it had "struck several military operatives".

Gaza health officials said another two people were killed on Thursday by Israeli fire in eastern Gaza City, according to Reuters. There was no immediate comment from the IDF.

At least 1,662 people have been killed in Israeli attacks in Gaza since the ceasefire began last year, according to the territory's Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the UN.

The Israeli military says six of its soldiers have been killed over the same period.

Meanwhile, more than 1.9 million people - about 90% of Gaza's population - remain displaced, with 1.4 million of them living in tents or makeshift shelters, according to the UN.

Reconstruction has yet to begin in Gaza, where an estimated 82% of all structures have been destroyed or damaged during the war, as US President Donald Trump's peace plan has largely stalled.

The disarmament of Hamas has been a key sticking point.

The group has agreed to give up its weapons in exchange for a phased withdrawal of Israeli troops from the 60% of Gaza they currently occupy. But Israel has insisted that Hamas must fully disarm before any pullout.

The war was triggered by the Hamas-led attack on southern Israel on 7 October 2023, when about 1,200 people were killed and 251 others were taken hostage.

Since then, more than 74,710 people have been killed in Israeli attacks in Gaza, its health ministry says.

articles.title: Putin vows 'far more painful' response to Ukraine's strikes on Crimean Bridge
articles.summary: The bridge - a symbol of Russia's occupation of the Crimean Peninsula - suffered major damaged following a combined attack by Ukraine earlier this week.
articles.preview: Moscow's retaliation for attacks on the Crimean Bridge will be "far more painful" than Kyiv's strikes, Vladimir Putin has vowed. In the early hours of Thursday, the double-arched, 12-mile bridge connecting Russia to Ukraine's occupied peninsula of Crimea was hit for a third time this week. A combined missile-and-drone strike on Tuesday destroyed the central road section of the bridge, collapsing part of it into the water and rendering it unusable for road traffic.
articles.body:
Moscow's retaliation for attacks on the Crimean Bridge will be "far more painful" than Kyiv's strikes, Vladimir Putin has vowed.

In the early hours of Thursday, the double-arched, 12-mile bridge connecting Russia to Ukraine's occupied peninsula of Crimea was hit for a third time this week.

A combined missile-and-drone strike on Tuesday destroyed the central road section of the bridge, collapsing part of it into the water and rendering it unusable for road traffic.

But at a press conference after historic talks with his Chinese and US counterparts in Shenzhen, Russian president Putin said Moscow's response would be even more significant.

Putin claimed the bridge was used exclusively for civilian purposes and not to transport military equipment, as Kyiv has alleged, or petroleum products.

Since illegally annexing the Crimean Peninsula in 2014, Moscow has used it as a military base, with airbases, troop concentrations, training grounds and artillery stockpiles.

From there it has also carried out strikes on the rest of the country and resupplied its troops in southern Ukraine.

Commenting on the strikes on the bridge, Kyiv's defence ministry said that for Ukraine, they amounted to to "time gained and lives saved. The less that reaches the occupiers, the less hits our warriors."

The collapse of the Crimean Bridge's arch was the worst damage to be inflicted onto the structure in several years.

The bridge had long been in Ukraine's sights because it represents Moscow's pretensions over sovereign Ukrainian land, and because of its logistical importance in supplying Russian troops in the occupied Ukrainian southern regions.

It was built and unveiled to great fanfare in 2018, four years after Russia illegally annexed Ukraine's Crimea.

Thursday's strike was carried out with Neptune cruise missiles, Ukraine said. Russia's transport ministry said nobody had been hurt in the attack, and that specialists were assessing damage to the bridge. Train services on the bridge were suspended but resumed in the afternoon.

Car traffic, however, will be prohibited for the foreseeable future as a section about 200m (660ft) long of the tarmac was dragged below into the sea when missiles hit the arch on Tuesday.

President Volodymyr Zelensky called the initial strikes on the Crimean Bridge an "unprecedented operation" weeks in the making.

The seven-stage operation first required the destruction of air defence systems, radars, electronic warfare assets which protected the bridge. Missiles and drones then dealt the structure the final blow.

In response to Tuesday's hit, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said the bridge "will be rebuilt, and it will be even better than before".

But the operation to repair it could take a long time, and it will likely have to be carried out under frequent Ukrainian fire.

Russia has regularly targeted Ukrainian civilian infrastructure since launching its full-scale invasion in 2022.

This week alone, as the Crimean Bridge was being hit, Moscow targeted key bridge crossings over the Dnipro River in Kyiv.

articles.title: Myanmar committed genocide against Rohingya, top UN court rules
articles.summary: The International Court of Justice has upheld large parts of a genocide case against Myanmar linked to the 2017 conflict with its Rohingya minority. It called for it to pay reparations and let refugees return safely.
articles.preview: November 19, 2026 The International Court of Justice has upheld large parts of a genocide case against Myanmar linked to the 2017 conflict with its Rohingya minority. It called for it to pay reparations and let refugees return safely. The International Court of Justice (ICJ) on Thursday found Myanmar in breach of several of its obligations under international treaties to prevent and not to commit genocide.
articles.body:
November 19, 2026

The International Court of Justice has upheld large parts of a genocide case against Myanmar linked to the 2017 conflict with its Rohingya minority. It called for it to pay reparations and let refugees return safely.

The International Court of Justice (ICJ) on Thursday found Myanmar in breach of several of its obligations under international treaties to prevent and not to commit genocide.

The ICJ's president, Judge Yuji Iwasawa said that the panel of 15 judges had decided by nine votes to six that Myanmar had committed genocide against the Rohingya in Rakhine state.

The judges also found the country guilty of a series of other more specific violations by majority rulings.

"On the basis of all the evidence taken together, the Court is of the view that the only reasonable inference that can explain Myanmar's actions is an intention to destroy a substantial part of... the Rohingya population in northern Rakhine State," ICJ President Yuji Iwasawa said.

Iwasawa said that Myanmar should make efforts to pay reparations to victims or their associates where possible and appropriate.

He also called for it to facilitate the safe return of refugees, and to take measures to investigate and, if necessary, prosecute individual wrongdoing by its nationals and security forces.

What Judge Iwasawa said as he read out the verdict against Myanmar

The ICJ said in its consideration, the Rohingya constituted a distinct ethnic group with their own defining language and culture, as well as self-identifying as such. This means they qualified as a protected group for the purposes of international laws against genocide.

Myanmar's security forces "killed thousands of Rohingya civilians, perpetrated acts of sexual violence, as well as extreme violence against children," and also attacked Rohingya as they tried to flee the fighting, the ICJ's Iwasawa said.

"The court is fully convinced that the 2017 clearance operations caused serious bodily and mental harm to a significant number of the protected group," Judge Iwasawa said.

Iwasawa also said that some civilian participation in the clearance operations could not necessarily be considered state-ordered or state-sanctioned behavior. But the court found that the government and security forces also made no meaningful efforts to prevent non-Rohingya civilian atrocities and fanned the flames of ethnic and religious tension.

At one point, reading the details of the findings, Iwasawa noted "Myanmar's failure, genuinely to investigate the alleged atrocities, and its refusal to facilitate access to evidence and witnesses, or provide information requested."

He said this meant it was possible the court did not have reliable knowledge of information available only from within Myanmar to which it was not given access.

How did groups from Myanmar respond?

There was no immediate response from the government in Myanmar or the military, which is regarded as the real underlying power.

Rohingya activist Yasmin Ullah — a Canadian citizen since 2016 but who was born in Rakhine state and who was a member of Gambia's delegation that filed the ICJ case — called the verdict more important for the world than for her community.

"The Rohingya never needed a court to tell us what happened to us," she said. "We needed the world to hear it, and today it has."

Wai Wai Nu, a Rohingya activist who directs the Women's Peace Network NGO, said the world's highest court's finding followed "decades" when "the Burmese military tried to erase our identity, deny our existence and dismiss our suffering."

And the co-chair of the Arakan Rohingya National Council, Nay San Lwin, said that for Rohingya people, "justice means the restoration of our citizenship, recognition of our identity and our safe and dignified return home."

Myanmar's shadow national unity government, which includes remnants of former President Aung San Suu Kyi's National League for Democracy Party, said it "respects the authority" of the ICJ.

It said that since the beginning of the "revolution against military dictatorship" in 2021, it had affirmed its "commitment to the rule of law, human rights, justice and states' obligations to prevent and punish genocide."

Myanmar was under nominally civilian rule at the time of the atrocities, but the extent to which Suu Kyi's government held sway over the military and its actions is debatable.

How did the international community react?

UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres welcomed Thursday's verdict, calling it a "powerful recognition of the Rohingya victims of genocide" and noting it was the first verdict of its kind against a state.

"Myanmar must act in accordance with its obligation to comply with the Court's decision," Guterres said in a statement, adding that this includes "the safe, voluntary and dignified return [of Rohingya] to their place of residence nad reunification of families."

Gambia's Justice Minister Dawda Jallow, who attended the hearing, spoke to reporters afterward at the Peace Palace in The Hague.

"The victory belongs to the Rohingya," Jallow said. "They survived. They testified. And today, they will believe."

UK Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband issued a statement saying the former colonial power was "taking immediate action today in light of this judgment."

Miliband said Britain would expel Myanmar's defense attache in London and was calling for a special UN Security Council session in response. He called on Myanmar to "comply fully with the judgment," and on the international community to "play its part in supporting implementation, accountability, and justice for the Rohingya."

UN human rights chief Volker Türk said the ruling "clearly concludes the State of Myanmar stands responsible for one of the most egregious crimes known to humankind."

What is the genocide case against Myanmar?

The case centers around the military crackdown in Rakhine state on the country's western coastline against the predominantly Muslim Rohingya minority in 2017.

Violence had been brewing for several years beforehand, but the most intense phase of the military crackdown in the north of region was triggered by a coordinated attack by a Muslim militia group against several police and military installations and personnel in August 2017.

A UN fact finding mission later concluded that some 10,000 people likely died in the military clearance operations that followed. Around 700,000 people fled to Bangladesh, where most still reside in the world's largest refugee camp.

Gambia filed the complaint at The Hague in 2019, alleging a deliberate campaign of arson, rape and murder designed to wipe out the Rohingya minority in whole or in part.

Myanmar's influential military, now back in full de facto control of the country albeit amid a long-running civil war, has maintained that it was engaged in a legitimate counterinsurgency.

Aung San Suu Kyi, who was the civilian president at the time, took a slightly more nuanced stance, but nevertheless traveled to The Hague to contest the charges, calling them "incomplete and incorrect."

The case is likely to draw close attention from those pursuing ICJ prosecutions against Israel and Benjamin Netanyahu for the war in Gaza and against Russia and Vladimir Putin for the invasion of Ukraine.

articles.title: Apple may be developing its own AI agent that runs your Mac
articles.summary: The iPhone maker appears to be building agents that can compete with the likes of Meta Muse, Instinct, Claude, and OpenAI Dots.
articles.preview: Apple appears to be working on its own AI agent to conduct computer work on behalf of users — including using apps, accessing websites, and coding, among other things. The news was originally reported by Bloomberg, which spotted a job listing the iPhone maker recently posted for a senior engineering manager to oversee the creation of an “AI agent that can use a computer.” “Imagine an AI agent that can use a computer the way a capable person does,” the posting says.
articles.body:
Apple appears to be working on its own AI agent to conduct computer work on behalf of users — including using apps, accessing websites, and coding, among other things.

The news was originally reported by Bloomberg, which spotted a job listing the iPhone maker recently posted for a senior engineering manager to oversee the creation of an “AI agent that can use a computer.”

“Imagine an AI agent that can use a computer the way a capable person does,” the posting says. “It browses the web, works across apps, runs commands, writes and debugs code, and calls services, and it chooses the right tool for each step. It does all this privately and with the polish people expect from Apple.”

The posting additionally notes that the agents should be able to move “fluidly between tools” and “carry out multi-step tasks across apps, browsers, command lines, code, and APIs.”

TechCrunch reached out to Apple for more information but did not receive a response.

Agents capable of computer work have become one of the hottest commodities in the tech industry over the past year. Major labs like Anthropic and OpenAI have launched such services, while other major tech brands — like Meta, which recently launched its Muse agent line — have also moved into the space. It makes sense that Apple — which is trying to expand its AI offerings in the new John Ternus era — would want to follow suit.

Bloomberg additionally notes that, at the same time that Apple is working on its own digital assistant, the company is making it significantly harder for third-party agents to gain total control over its computers.

The outlet notes that the version of its upcoming macOS 27.3 will deploy warnings discouraging users from granting full access to third-party agents. In October, Apple issued a notification to developers stating that the company planned to “introduce additional controls to ensure that users who genuinely wish to grant an app this extraordinary level of access can only do so with very explicit user action.”

Bloomberg writes that while the iPhone maker “has eyed introducing the service as soon as the end of next year,” progress on its in-house agent “remains in the early stages.”

articles.title: Anthropic’s 7 founders cashed out nearly $2B in record-breaking IPO
articles.summary: At the upgraded $83/share IPO price, Anthropic's seven founders each pocketed $280 million, while the company nabbed nearly $105 billion.
articles.preview: Anthropic became a public company on Thursday, raising a total of $81.3 billion, including $1.95 billion for its seven founders. As we previously reported, each of them ponied up about 3.4 million shares apiece to sell in the IPO. At the upgraded IPO price of $83 per share, that means they each pocketed about $280 million before underwriting fees and taxes. It looked like they had calculated the number of shares they planned to sell to give them each around $250 million if shares hit $74. That was the midpoint price from Anthropic’s original price range.
articles.body:
Anthropic became a public company on Thursday, raising a total of $81.3 billion, including $1.95 billion for its seven founders. As we previously reported, each of them ponied up about 3.4 million shares apiece to sell in the IPO.

At the upgraded IPO price of $83 per share, that means they each pocketed about $280 million before underwriting fees and taxes. It looked like they had calculated the number of shares they planned to sell to give them each around $250 million if shares hit $74. That was the midpoint price from Anthropic’s original price range. So that’s a cool $30-ish million more for each of them than perhaps they were gunning for.

Anthropic implied in its IPO filings that the founders aren’t entirely in this for the money though. The company said that each of the founders has pledged to dedicate 80% of their personal equity in the company to philanthropy.

However, if any of them struggle to live on their quarter of a billion, they can scale back their charitable commitments. The company points out that these commitments are “voluntary, revocable expressions of each co-founder’s philanthropic intent and do not constitute legally binding obligations.”

With the IPO in the record books, there were a few other interesting numbers worth highlighting.

$104.8 billion. That’s really the amount Anthropic raised for its coffers (with a possibility of $117 billion, if the bankers buy all of their allotment of shares). In addition to selling its Class A common stock, it also sold a previously announced $26 billion worth of a special non-voting Class N stock to some of the biggest tech names in the industry.

Nvidia bought $10 billion of these Class N shares, Google bought $10 billion, and AMD, Broadcom, Micron, Microsoft, and TSMC divvied up the rest.

Just for comparison: When Facebook had its then record-breaking IPO in 2012, it raised $16 billion on IPO day.

28% stake to Amazon and Google combined. All told, at the higher IPO share price, Google wound up owning 13.4% of the company. Amazon also now has a big stake in Anthropic because when it previously invested in the AI lab as a startup, it was granted promissory notes that could be converted to equity. It converted a small percentage of them as part of the IPO, leaving it with a 14.6% stake. Had it converted all of them, Amazon could have owned nearly 24%.

The two large cloud providers now own 28% of Anthropic, the AI lab says.

More than $1 trillion. As mind-blowing as it is to raise nearly $105 billion, giving Anthropic nearly $230 billion of working capital available (along with capital it already had on hand), the company’s need for future capital is still far greater.

Anthropic needs about $70.7 billion just to cover its compute and infrastructure spending commitments in the next 12 months as of the quarter ended September 30, 2026. It needs $451.6 billion to cover these commitments before the end of 2030. And it has racked up hundreds of billions of other commitments that are either conditional (and may not happen) or haven’t been priced yet.

All told, the company has disclosed a ballpark of $1.05 trillion to $1.08 trillion in infrastructure commitments in its foreseeable future. This was a huge IPO. But it is a pricey business to run.

articles.title: Anthropic rival says companies can (mostly) skip the pricey models
articles.summary: On the day Anthropic went public, Fireworks AI’s co-founder made the case for open source models as a cheaper alternative, and addressed the breaches that have cost the company some customers’ trust.
articles.preview: On the same day that Anthropic went public in the largest IPO on record, with investor enthusiasm for the AI lab through the roof, far away at the Slush startup conference in Helsinki, the topic du jour was open source everything. That’s the enormous opportunity being chased by companies like Fireworks AI, as enterprises seek ways to avoid paying frontier prices for their AI needs. Fireworks runs AI models for other businesses.
articles.body:
On the same day that Anthropic went public in the largest IPO on record, with investor enthusiasm for the AI lab through the roof, far away at the Slush startup conference in Helsinki, the topic du jour was open source everything.

That’s the enormous opportunity being chased by companies like Fireworks AI, as enterprises seek ways to avoid paying frontier prices for their AI needs.

Fireworks runs AI models for other businesses. It specializes in open-weight models, which anyone can download, and helps customers tune them on their own data so they run faster and cheaper than the models of Anthropic, OpenAI, and other heavyweights, and are harder for rivals to copy. Customers have included Uber, Shopify, and Notion. Co-founder Chenyu Zhao and I spoke onstage toward the end of the day.

Zhao and many others believe companies are gravitating toward platforms like his because frontier models are pricey and, in most cases, he says, unnecessary unless you need the very latest and greatest generalized intelligence. There are also growing concerns that frontier labs absorb too much of their customers’ know-how, even if only through the prompts used to get answers, a worry Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella raised in July.

Fireworks has also gotten its first black eye, having disclosed two security incidents this fall. In one, hackers reached API keys and tokens stored as secrets for a limited number of accounts; in the other, attackers breached its cloud provider, made their way into a development system, and nabbed customer data, including billing records and some datasets.

Notion says AI chat transcripts from fewer than 1% of its workspaces were exposed, but it has disconnected from Fireworks. Uber says hackers stole the names, addresses, birth dates and driver’s license numbers of about 150,000 drivers through a vendor that TechCrunch identified as Fireworks. Fireworks will have to win back the confidence of customers like them.

Fireworks, assigned a $17.5 billion valuation by its investors in summer, is reportedly in “early talks” for yet another round, though Zhao declined to comment.

There’s money chasing everyone in the category, seems like. Rival companies Together AI and Baseten have announced massive rounds in recent months. On Wednesday, Palo Alto Networks said it will buy Applied Compute, which, like Fireworks, helps companies train and run custom AI models on their own data. The deal for the startup, founded just a year ago by former OpenAI researchers, is $4.5 billion, all of it in stock.

Here’s some of what Zhao had to say. This conversation has been edited for length and clarity.

You spent a decade at Google, including managing a 50-person engineering team on Google Cloud Vertex AI. Why leave when you did?

When you meet great co-founders, it’s obvious within five minutes that they’re really smart. I was sold after talking to Lin [Qiao] and Dima [Dzhulgakov]. It’s also important to find people who are genuinely nice, people you’ll enjoy working with.

How do you describe Fireworks to a CEO who has never heard of it?

I describe Fireworks as a specialized intelligence platform. OpenAI and Anthropic are building general intelligence. We use open models, which are often smaller, cheaper, and faster, and let companies add their own data to specialize them. That way you own your AI rather than being beholden to giant AI conglomerates. If you’re just using Opus or Sonnet, that’s not a differentiator.

How far behind are open models right now?

A few years ago I’d have said a year, a year and a half. Then came DeepSeek and a waterfall of fantastic open models. These days it’s at most six months behind, probably closer to three.

If the models are so close behind, why are businesses slow to switch?

Frontier models are a household brand, and before you find product-market fit, using the best model is low risk. But once you pass 10,000 or 100,000 users and you’re spending $10,000 to $100,000 a month on tokens, it’s time to think about open source.

In July, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella warned that companies using proprietary AI models pay twice, once in money and again in know-how. Do you think that warning had a material effect?

We think we’ll live in a two-model world, with frontier and open models in parallel. You want the best intelligence for high-level planning, but you don’t need a frontier model for basic arithmetic. That’s why there’s so much interest in routing, and why people now think about cost per task, not just cost per token.

Anthropic went public today. What do you think of its valuation? There’s one scenario in which it just continues to cement its place in this sort of oligopoly; there’s another where it starts to lose traction.

On the record: I’ll probably call my broker tonight and buy a few shares. This is a long-term bet. In 10 years AI usage will be at a completely different scale, and that takes an incredible amount of capital, which is why these companies are going public.

Fireworks has had a couple of security breaches recently. What do you tell customers?

Every company is probably seeing an unprecedented frequency of attacks. For our incident, a lot of the motivation was LLM jacking: hunting through providers for API keys and secrets to sell tokens on illicit marketplaces. Our promise is zero data retention for inference traffic, and there’s no indication that has been compromised.

Notion has disconnected from Fireworks. Did you lose other customers?

I don’t think I can publicly name the specific customers that were impacted. Some, such as Notion and Cursor, have gone public already. It was a small subset of our customers that had this data impact.

How did that customer data get exposed, given your zero-retention promise?

Notion was using batch prediction, where you upload a dataset that’s stored at rest, so it’s not a zero-retention product by nature. We’re moving those services to an online flow so we keep data only as long as we need it.

Jensen Huang left Nvidia last week, and Nvidia has backed Fireworks since 2024. Does that affect you?

It’s been a blow to the industry, and we feel for Jensen and his family. But Nvidia has always been a strong supporter of open source, and I don’t see that changing. We expect it to keep investing in Nemotron, and we’re excited to keep partnering with them.

articles.title: Anthropic becomes one of world's most valuable public companies in stock market debut
articles.summary: Anthropic is the first purely AI company to be publicly listed, creating a test for the entire industry.
articles.preview: Anthropic has become one of the most valuable public companies in the world after its shares began trading on the stock market, taking its valuation to roughly $1.76 trillion (£1.34 trillion). The artificial intelligence (AI) company's Thursday debut on the Nasdaq stock exchange was a crucial test for the industry, given the huge amount of money being poured into advancing the technology. Anthropic's shares flew past its allocation price of $83 each, showing there was plenty of excitement around AI.
articles.body:
Anthropic has become one of the most valuable public companies in the world after its shares began trading on the stock market, taking its valuation to roughly $1.76 trillion (£1.34 trillion).

The artificial intelligence (AI) company's Thursday debut on the Nasdaq stock exchange was a crucial test for the industry, given the huge amount of money being poured into advancing the technology.

Anthropic's shares flew past its allocation price of $83 each, showing there was plenty of excitement around AI.

Yet the company, which is behind AI chatbot Claude, will remain under intense scrutiny in the months ahead to answer the key question surrounding AI: is it all worth it?

In just a few hours of trading, Anthropic's stock seemed to show that investors remain uncertain of where exactly AI is heading. The share price rose immediately to $111.53, sending the company's market value to almost $2 trillion, before falling by the end of the day as the shares closed at $97.17.

Some investors said Anthropic's debut seemed to be a success, as shares rose roughly 17% during the day, but the broader tech market did not perform as well.

The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite Index closed down nearly 2.3%. Stocks fell in the largest tech firms, including Google's parent company Alphabet, which was down by 2.9%, while Amazon lost almost 3.9%.

The buildout happening around this era of AI is among the most expensive endeavours in the history of technology, with more than $1 trillion being spent in the last year alone by a handful of major tech companies.

The speed at which investment has grown has led to ongoing concerns of a financial bubble.

"Bubbles don't burst on the day of the largest deal," Richard Whittle, an economist with the University of Salford said. "They burst later, if the positive future becomes suspect."

While the basics of the technology have been around for decades, the more recent advent of more powerful computers and related components have allowed the processing of more data than ever.

The result has been AI chatbots that simulate human speech and operate tasks like software coding, digital image generation, and searching the internet more quickly.

It represents a new way of using computers that has led to the rapid rise of Anthropic, which started just five years ago and is best known as the maker of the popular AI chatbot Claude.

As the first purely AI company to go public, Anthropic will almost certainly see significant swings in price on the stock market going forward, according to Ben Barringer, who leads technology research at Quilter Cheviot.

The "initial exuberance" will wear off, Barringer said, pointing to what happened with SpaceX earlier this year.

That company, led by Elon Musk, saw shares jump by about 10% on the first day of trading, taking the company to a record-breaking valuation of $2.2 trillion.

Within a month shares had fallen below their debut price, and have mostly fallen further since.

Most tech companies see their shares fall after hitting the stock market, often after reporting quarterly results for the first time.

But many such companies, including Meta, Amazon and Google, have gone on to become the largest and most profitable corporations in the world.

With Anthropic, investors are not only looking at a notable tech company with a major valuation, and a potentially big future in business, but a company that is the first of its kind on the stock market.

"There's no obvious peer to compare it to," Neil Wilson, an investor strategist at Saxo UK, said.

So, as individual investors and even researchers and investors at large funds ask themselves if Anthropic is really worth more than $1.7 trillion, or even more, there will be few answers available.

"We'll have a stab at it," Wilson said. "I don't think anyone really knows."

A few things will likely impact the company's success on the stock market in the near-term.

One of those things is the prospect of new laws governing the use of AI tools. In the US, where Anthropic is based, Democrats will be in many more positions of power come 2027, and several politicians have already said they will be looking to ensure AI tools are safe and have some guardrails attached.

Such regulation is currently unlikely at the federal level. US President Donald Trump on Thursday spoke about AI during the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in China, alongside Chinese and Russian counterparts, Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin.

Trump reiterated his position against "any form of robust regulation" around the technology, adding, "we won't allow that to happen, frankly."

The same day, however, a bipartisan group of US lawmakers formed the House AI Safety and Innovation Caucus, which will work specifically on AI regulation and safety considerations.

A significant driver of this kind of scrutiny is Anthropic itself. Company executives, including co-founder and CEO Dario Amodei, have been outspoken in their purported fears that future AI tools will become so capable they will outsmart humans, to the point where extinction is possible.

Anthropic has always put itself forward in public as an AI company that takes the safety of its technology very seriously.

Daniela Amodei, Anthropic's president and sister of Dario Amodei, boasted on Thursday that the company "had an AI safety team before we launched our first product".

"AI carries real risks," she added.

Despite the company's claims that the technology it is building at a rapid pace could be dangerous, Anthropic has made one of the quickest trips from start-up to IPO in history.

- Published11 hours ago

articles.summary: "We've got this," Colette Kress, interim CEO of Nvidia, said Tuesday night as she closed out the embattled chip company's third quarter earnings call. By Thursday, the company's stock price was hovering at around $150 per share, a nearly 40 percent drop from its all-time high on October 6th, and wiping out a brief post-earnings
articles.body:
“We’ve got this,” Colette Kress, interim CEO of Nvidia, said Tuesday night as she closed out the embattled chip company’s third quarter earnings call.

Tracking the stock price amid Jensen Huang’s extramarital affairs and alleged spy scandal.

By Thursday, the company’s stock price was hovering at around $150 per share, a nearly 40 percent drop from its all-time high on October 6th, and wiping out a brief post-earnings pop on Tuesday night. Meanwhile, Wall Street was paying up for one of Nvidia’s biggest customers as Anthropic made its Nasdaq debut at $111.50 per share — 34 percent higher than expected.

Looking at the earnings report numbers alone, Nvidia had a blockbuster quarter. Q3 revenue more than doubled from the same period last year up to total $115.8 billion, driven by data center revenue that was up 110 percent and exceeding Wall Street expectations. Nearly $20 billion in revenue came from the highly anticipated Vera Rubin platform, which shipped during the quarter, becoming the “fastest product ramp in company history,” Kress told investors.

“Our momentum is real,” Kress said. “With the market-leading multiyear roadmap, supply agreements extending through to the end of the decade, and sustainable demand, we are well positioned to accelerate Nvidia’s leadership position.”

But investors are stilltrying to reconcile Nvidia’s stellar recent financial performance and position as a central pillar in the AI economy with serious concerns over its future.

The company’s stock has taken a stunning tumble in recent weeks. Fueled first by a broader market sell-off of chip stocks amid concerns about the AI bubble, the stock took another blow following the resignation of former CEO Jensen Huang amid reports of extramarital affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese spy, according to US intelligence sources cited by The New York Times.

Harvey Jones, Nvidia’s newly appointed chairman of the board, told investors on the call Tuesday that the company “does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO” and has already tapped an executive search firm to help find a replacement. Huang, who cofounded Nvidia in 1993 and has led the company ever since — famously without a succession plan — has become essentially inseparable from it in the eyes of Wall Street and the media. But while Huang may not be ready to let go, posting on X this week that he’d be “honored” to be reinstated as CEO, Nvidia’s executive suite seems ready to move on.

It has been a tumultuous two and a half weeks for Nvidia.

On October 29th, The New York Times reported that US intelligence agencies believed Jensen Huang to be the target of a Chinese espionage plot. The report centered on his “close relationship” with Alice Huang, a Chinese national and an executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based data center company and one of Nvidia’s clients. Nvidia initially contested the report, adding that Jensen Huang’s interactions with Alice Huang “are not unusual or unexpected.”

Nvidia’s stock seemingly remained unaffected by the reports, at least at first. The share price closed at $213.66 on October 29th, down just 0.8 percent from the previous day. (Julian Barnes, one of the reporters on the story, later commented, “I will confess I was kind of surprised that the world’s initial reaction to our October story was a bit muted.”) The stock closed at a 4 percent drop the next day as the entire Nasdaq fell 2.9 percent, the worst single-day decline since June.

The stock continued to fall through Wednesday, November 4th, the day after the blue wave swept the midterms, stoking fears on Wall Street that the new class of Democratic governors in key states like Texas would slow down data center construction. On Thursday, November 5th, Nvidia’s stock fell 9.2 percent, its largest single-day drop in at least a year. But chip stocks began to recover the next day, and by close on Friday, November 6th, Nvidia was back up 2.8 percent to a share price of $186.64.

Then all hell broke loose. On Sunday, November 8th, Jensen Huang sent a company-wide memo to Nvidia staff in which he apologized for engaging in an extramarital affair. The memo coincided with the opening of an independent investigation by Nvidia’s board into Huang’s alleged misconduct and whether company secrets or national security had been compromised. Huang said he would cooperate fully with the investigation. By the opening bell on Monday, November 9th, Nvidia shares had tumbled 7 percent and trading volume surged past its three-month average as investors reacted to the memo. After a brief rebound, the stock continued to oscillate the next day, as more details of Jensen Huang and Alice Huang’s relationship emerged. By the time the market closed on Tuesday, November 10th, Nvidia shares were down to $168.89, nearly 10 percent below the closing price on the last day of 2025.

The stock rebounded slightly on Wednesday, November 11th, as investors prepared for Nvidia’s third quarter earnings call, scheduled for the following Tuesday, November 17th. By Wednesday night, however, shares had plunged yet again as media reports circulated that Nvidia’s board was considering ousting Huang, and other reports emerged detailing a second alleged affair, this time between Huang and an Nvidia employee.

Nvidia announced Huang’s departure on the morning of Thursday, November 12th, sending the company’s shares falling nearly 14 percent at the open. It closed at just a 4.3 percent dip. The intraday low of $148.80 per share was its lowest price in a year.

On December 1st, Jensen Huang will appear before the House Foreign Affairs Committee, the Select Committee on the Chinese Communist Party, and the House Intelligence Committee for transcribed interviews. Nvidia’s general counsel will do the same on December 2nd.

Retail investors have already seized the opportunity to buy the dip. In the first 30 minutes of trading on Thursday, November 12th, retail investors bought $111 million of Nvidia shares in the largest-ever first half-hour of opening for the stock, Bloomberg reported, citing Vanda Research.

They might be onto something.

Nvidia’s average price target is $232.59, with the lowest estimate at $130 and the highest at $350, according to an analysis of analyst projections over the last three months by Google Finance.

Nearly two-thirds of those analysts issued a “Buy” rating for Nvidia in the last three months. Of those, all 30 reiterated that rating post-earnings.

The stock closed at $145.98 on Thursday, a new 52-week low.

Then again, numbers are the core basis for stock market ratings, and numbers may not be Nvidia’s problem right now. It’s everything else — the leadership vacuum, upcoming congressional testimony, regulatory uncertainty, broader questions about neocloud customer financing and sales to China — that will continue to impact the stock in the coming weeks.

Anthropic ha archiviato al sua prima seduta in rialzo del 17% a 97,17 dollari per un valore di circa 1.300 miliardi, o 1.760 miliardi su base diluita. Un balzo che non è bastato a Wall Street.

I listini americani hanno chiuso in rosso per la sesta giornata consecutiva. Il Dow Jones ha perso il 2,19% scendendo sotto quota 50.000 punti e il Nasdaq il 2,25%. Lo S&P 500 è sceso del 2,02%, in quella che la sua più lunga serie di perdite dal 2024. Con il boom della quotazione, i sette fondatori di Anthropic - tutti ex dipendenti di OpenAI - diventano multimiliardari, arrivando a valere più di 20 miliardi ciascuno.

A festeggiare sono però anche i dipendenti della società, che grazie all'operazione possono contare su una ricchezza media di 44 milioni a persona. Grandi profitti anche per le banche che hanno curato l'ipo, con la quale sono stati raccolti 81,3 miliardi di dollari tramite la vendita di 980 milioni di azioni a 83 dollari l'una. Agli istituti infatti andranno complessivamente 550 milioni di dollari in commissioni, meno dell'1% del totale raccolto. Morgan Stanley e Goldman Sachs incasseranno complessivamente il 41% del totale, circa 110 milioni ciascuna.

Cifre stellari che confermano l'appetito degli investitori per l'intelligenza artificiale nonostante le recenti difficoltà dovute allo scandalo di Nvidia e ai timori di una bolla che possa a breve scoppiare. Suonando la campanella dell'avvio degli scambi al Nasdaq, l'amministratore delegato Dario Amodei è apparso visibilmente emozionato e contento. "Non cederemo né alle pressioni commerciali né a quelle politiche", ha detto in un breve discorso assicurando che Anthropic resterà "ossessionata" dalla sicurezza dell'IA.

"Oggi mettiamo l'azienda in una posizione finanziaria più solida" e questo "rafforza ulteriormente la nostra determinazione ad agire nel modo giusto", ha spiegato Amodei, finito nei mesi scorsi al centro di uno scontro con il Pentagono sulle limitazioni all'uso dell'intelligenza artificiale che Anthropic aveva imposto, affermandosi come uno dei paladini dello sviluppo di un'IA sicura e che porti benefici a tutti.

Il ceo di origini italiane - suo padre Riccardo Amodei era un artigiano pellettiere - è stato tra i primi a chiedere un rallentamento dello sviluppo dell'intelligenza artificiale e a mettere in guardia sui rischi di estinzione dell'umanità. Una posizione la sua condivisa anche da Elon Musk, che ha lodato la società. "Conosco molte persone che ci lavorano, avendole incontrate ai miei tempi a OpenAI. Per quello che può valere, nessuno di loro mi ha fatto scattare il 'rilevatore della malvagità'", ha detto il patron di Tesla che ha un contenzioso aperto con Sam Altman, il numero uno di OpenAI.

Il successo dell'ipo apre un nuovo capitolo nell'era dell'IA finora rimasta protetta dai riflettori finanziari, e arriva fra il crescente scetticismo degli americani nei confronti della nuova tecnologia. Una frustrazione evidente nelle proteste fuori dal Nasdaq durante la quotazione di Anthropic, con striscioni contro i miliardari tech e alcuni arresti. Le elezioni di metà mandato hanno infatti rivelato che gli elettori sono contrari ad avere data center nelle loro comunità, e hanno paura degli effetti che l'IA potrebbe avere sul mercato del lavoro.

Secondo il presidente della Fed Kevin Warsh, il fenomeno va esaminato da vari punti di vista. Da un lato può infatti aumentare la produttività del lavoro, con benefici ampiamente condivisi. Allo stesso tempo, comporta rischi di destabilizzazione legati a soggetti malintenzionati. Non si può inoltre escludere che l'IA deluda e che le aziende non riescano a realizzare rendimenti adeguati sui loro investimenti. Un'ipotesi che, alla luce dell'esordio di Anthropic a Wall Street, sembra per ora lontana.

articles.body:
EU targeted in an AI-assisted cyberattack, spokesperson says

November 19, 2026

The European Commission was targeted by an "AI-generated cybercampaign," a spokesperson has said. This is the first time the bloc has publicly reported an AI-based cyberattack.

The European Commission confirmed on Thursday that it was targeted by a cyberattack through the use of AI tools.

The incident was detected on October 22 and there was no evidence of a data breach affecting Commission staff as a whole, European Commission spokesperson Thomas Regnier told reporters.

"This was an AI-generated cybercampaign," he added.

Regnier did not elaborate on the attack or name a perpetrator. He said the Commission "has taken the necessary steps in response."

This is the first time the bloc reported an AI-assisted cyberattack.

Disruption reportedly lasted 10 days

Regnier's statement came after Politico reported earlier on Thursday that the Commission had been targeted. The report said the cyberattack disrupted several systems for 10 days and might have compromised large amounts of personal data. The European Commission has roughly 33,000 employees.

The Commission then convened its highest-level internal crisis management body for an urgent meeting about the cyber incidents, according to Politico.

"We temporarily took down several applications, and most of them have since then been restored," Regnier said. He also stated that they did not detect any evidence of a data breach affecting Commission staff.

Recent hybrid attacks on supermarkets, air traffic controllers, blood banks and broadcasters across Europe have raised worries among leaders that this may be part of a coordinated attempt at hybrid warfare.

France summoned the Iranian ambassador last week over cyberattacks that caused supermarket freezers to defrost, but Tehran has denied any involvement.

articles.title: La Anthropic in borsa tra miliardi e promesse
articles.summary: L’azienda ha raccolto 81 miliardi di dollari. I fondatori ne hanno blindato il controllo, con un accentramento del potere che fa sorgere molti dubbi
articles.preview: Il 19 novembre 2026 l’azienda d’intelligenza artificiale (ia) Anthropic ha fatto il suo debutto alla borsa statunitense, anticipando quello della rivale OpenAi, che pure era stata la prima protagonista del settore grazie al lancio di ChatGpt quattro anni fa. I numeri sono da capogiro: la Anthropic, artefice del chatbot Claude, ha venduto 980 milioni di azioni a 83 dollari l’una, cioè una quantità più alta del previsto (la stima era di 825 milioni) a un prezzo più alto di quello che tutti si aspettavano a Wall street (70-78 dollari).
articles.body:
Il 19 novembre 2026 l’azienda d’intelligenza artificiale (ia) Anthropic ha fatto il suo debutto alla borsa statunitense, anticipando quello della rivale OpenAi, che pure era stata la prima protagonista del settore grazie al lancio di ChatGpt quattro anni fa.

I numeri sono da capogiro: la Anthropic, artefice del chatbot Claude, ha venduto 980 milioni di azioni a 83 dollari l’una, cioè una quantità più alta del previsto (la stima era di 825 milioni) a un prezzo più alto di quello che tutti si aspettavano a Wall street (70-78 dollari).

L’operazione ha fruttato 81 miliardi di dollari, dando vita al più ricco collocamento in borsa di sempre e attestando il valore dell’Anthropic sui 1.500 miliardi. Altri 26 miliardi potrebbero arrivare da un gruppo di grandi investitori, tra cui la Nvidia e Google, attraverso una vendita privata. Un risultato ancora più impressionante se si pensa che l’Anthropic è nata sei anni fa.

La buona riuscita del collocamento in un certo senso interrompe i giorni cupi vissuti dal settore dell’ia in seguito alla scandalo della Nvidia e alle dimissioni del suo amministratore delegato Jensen Huang. E offre una pausa al timore diffuso che stia per scoppiare un’enorme bolla finanziaria. La stessa Anthropic aveva ridimensionato le previsioni sul debutto in borsa, stimando di poter raggiungere un valore di duemila miliardi di dollari.

Invece gli investitori che hanno cercato di accaparrarsi il titolo della Anthropic sono stati moltissimi, al punto da lamentarsi perché le azioni disponibili erano troppo poche.

Un potere illimitato

Alla fine del 19 novembre l’Anthropic si è ritrovata con un “tesoretto” di circa 94 miliardi di dollari. Soldi ovviamente destinati ad arricchire gli azionisti, ma non solo: in buona parte – si parla di 71 miliardi – saranno investiti nei data center e in generale nello sviluppo di nuove tecnologie nel 2027. Ed entro il 2045 l’azienda conta di investire novecento miliardi.

Tuttavia, il lancio della Anthropic sulla più grande piazza finanziaria del mondo è anche una grande sfida per dimostrare la sua effettiva solidità e in generale la capacità del settore dell’ia di affermarsi superando tutti i dubbi che lo circondano, innanzitutto quelli sulla possibilità di continuare a costruire data center in giro per il mondo e realizzare attività redditizie e davvero utili alle persone.

Fin dalla sua fondazione l’Anthropic ha sempre registrato perdite, anche se nei primi nove mesi del 2026 il suo fatturato è cresciuto del 1.200 per cento, arrivando a 33 miliardi di dollari. Ma ciò che più colpisce del suo collocamento è una decisione presa alla vigilia del suo ingresso del mondo del profitto a tutti i costi.

Lo spiega il settimanale tedesco Die Zeit: “L’azienda sostiene di essersi data un particolare meccanismo di tutela: una forma di separazione dei poteri per frenare la ricerca del profitto. In modo che l’ia della Anthropic continui a svilupparsi ‘a lungo termine a beneficio dell’umanità’”. Sarebbe un fatto senza precedenti, in effetti.

Nel prospetto della quotazione l’amministratore delegato Dario Amodei e gli altri sei fondatori dell’Anthropic hanno scritto che la loro ia potrebbe portare nel mondo sia cose positive sia cose negative: l’eradicazione di alcune malattie e una crescita economica senza precedenti; ma anche la creazione di sistemi di sorveglianza repressivi o consigli utili ai terroristi per la produzione di armi biologiche.

Per questo sentono la responsabilità di “aiutare il mondo a comprendere questi rischi e a prevenirli o mitigarli, qualora dovessero emergere dai nostri modelli d’ia”.

Sarà anche per questo che Amodei e i suoi soci hanno tenuto per sé una speciale categoria di azioni, denominata di classe F, che in teoria gli permetterà di controllare l’azienda all’infinito. O almeno di non farla cadere nelle mani di investitori e fondi speculativi che portano avanti piani altamente redditizi ma potenzialmente dannosi.

Una sorta di versione “istituzionalizzata” del famoso motto don’t be evil che aveva Google, osserva la Zeit. Ma questo presuppone che il potere illimitato di Amodei e soci sarà usato sempre nel modo giusto, senza scaricare il peso di eventuali danni sul resto della società.

Si può pure credere nella loro buona fede, ma le vicende recenti di Jensen Huang, un manager della Silicon valley dai poteri quasi illimitati, non dovrebbero far dormire sonni tranquilli a nessuno. ◆

articles.body:
China

US President Donald Trump held bilateral meetings with both Russia's Vladimir Putin and China’s Xi Jingping on Thursday on the sidelines of the Apec Summit in Shenzhen.

The private talks come ahead of an historic three-way discussion between the leaders later in the day.

Russian state media is reporting that Putin was in an excellent mood after his 40-minute meeting with Trump, during which they discussed the Ukraine war.

Ahead of his one-on-one with Trump, Xi said he remained committed to working with Washington to steer ties between their countries on the “correct course”.

The US president, for his part, said he expected the meeting would be “productive” and the two countries have now split tariffs in a “fair way”.

While the full agenda for the talks has not been made public, there have been hints about what could be discussed.

This includes the wars in Ukraine and Iran, nuclear proliferation, trade tensions, and developments in artificial intelligence.

Analysts expect discussions between the three powerful men to be heavier in symbolism than concrete breakthroughs, despite the unprecedented nature of the meeting.

Trump is bogged down by his war with Iran that has choked oil supplies and pushed up consumer prices worldwide, while an ascendant China is looking to strengthen its hand in East Asia.

The summit has stoked fears that the three leaders may seek to divide the globe into spheres of influence, for example by making decisions impacting the fate of Ukraine over the heads of Kyiv or Europe.

Critics have also warned that the optics from the meeting will be damaging for the US president, but a win for both Xi and Putin.

Other world leaders attending the APEC meeting include Japan's Sanae Takaichi, South Korea's Lee Jae Myung, Canada's Mark Carney, and Australia's Anthony Albanese

articles.title: Is the AI bubble bursting just as Anthropic goes public?
articles.summary: The sharp sell-off in tech stocks after the US midterms and the Nvidia scandal has cast doubt on Anthropic's IPO. Yet with hundreds of billions still being invested, some think the AI party is still in full swing.
articles.preview: November 19, 2026 The sharp sell-off in tech stocks after the US midterms and the Nvidia scandal has cast doubt on Anthropic's IPO. Yet with hundreds of billions still being invested, some think the AI party is still in full swing. articles.body:
November 19, 2026

The sharp sell-off in tech stocks after the US midterms and the Nvidia scandal has cast doubt on Anthropic's IPO. Yet with hundreds of billions still being invested, some think the AI party is still in full swing.

Anthropic, the artificial intelligence (AI) giant, made its Nasdaq debut Thursday in the largest share sale on record.

The Claude maker offered 980 million shares for sale at $83 (€76), yet began trading 34% higher at $111.50.

The opening price values the five-year-old firm at around $2 trillion, well above market estimates of around $1.3 trillion.

Anthropic's public listing is being seen as a key test of investor appetite for AI, as stock prices have swung wildly in recent months.

2026 was meant to be the year Wall Street’s trillion-dollar bet on what US President Donald Trump calls superintelligence (SI) started paying off.

In the first half of the year, it did. Many AI stocks hit record highs as US hyperscalers like Google's Alphabet, Meta and Microsoft recorded bumper earnings.

AI doubts trigger market turbulence

The second half of 2026, however, has brought a lot more uncertainty.

While the stock of chipmaker Nvidia pushed even higher last month, many hyperscalers and chip or memory firms have seen erratic movements in their stock prices.

Then, after the Democrats won control of the United States Congress in the midterm elections earlier this month, technology stocks sold off again dramatically.

The Magnificent Seven — including Meta, Apple, Amazon and Tesla — lost more than $1 trillion in value in a single trading day.

In a further twist, the AI sector took another hit last week as Nvidia shares plunged nearly 10% over two days.

The sell-off followed revelations that CEO Jensen Huang had an affair with a woman reportedly suspected by US intelligence of being a Chinese spy.

Huang resigned from the chipmaker, sending Nvidia's shares lower still and prompting a campaign by current and former staffers, investors and other key figures in Silicon Valley to have him reinstated.

Questions over timing of Anthropic IPO

While OpenAI — the maker of ChatGPT — has delayed its public listing until next year, some analysts have been left scratching their heads at Anthropic's decision to proceed, even though the IPO is reportedly about six times oversubscribed.

"Is this the best timing?" asked Dennis Dick, chief market strategist at the Canada-based Stock Trader Network, in an interview with DW last week.

Dick said Anthropic's valuation depends on whether it can deliver on a forecast by Goldman Sachs of more than $600 billion in revenue by 2030.

"If you get to a company with $600 billion in revenue, [a] $1.3 trillion [valuation] doesn’t sound that bad," he told DW. "But when you’re talking about a company with currently $52 billion in revenue, it sounds like it’s overvalued."

Other analysts, like Vivek Seth, chief executive officer of Shaires Holdings, are more bullish about the Claude maker's prospects.

"Anthropic is a once-in-a-generation company," Seth told Bloomberg last week, noting how it has grown rapidly and has strong institutional backing. "Its IPO will establish a market-clearing valuation as conditions stabilize."

Amid huge spending, big returns remain elusive

Wall Street is growing increasingly cautious about the sheer size of the AI outlay, amid warnings that future earnings may not justify the huge spending.

In September, investment bank Goldman Sachs estimated that hyperscalers need around $300 billion in annual AI revenue to break even on their spending, leaving a gap of roughly $230 billion.

"We're not in Kansas anymore," Dick quipped, borrowing a line from the classic movie "The Wizard of Oz," which means times have changed. Now, he said, investors are telling companies: "Show me the money."

AI stocks needed a 'healthy correction'

Other analysts, however, think it's too soon to expect the AI bubble to burst, including Kit Rees, investment strategist at London-based wealth manager Quilter, who thinks the post-election rout was a "healthy correction."

"We’re still in the very early innings of the AI build-out," Rees told DW. "There’s still a lot of excitement around this technology and investors will want to have a slice of the pie."

In addition to the roughly $800 billion invested in capital expenditures this year, AI hyperscalers plan to spend a further $1.2 trillion in 2027 and $1.4 trillion in 2028, according to Goldman Sachs estimates.

Signs to watch, not reasons to flee

With many investors already running for the hills, Rees isn’t convinced the AI bubble will burst in the way skeptics expect. She thinks they should watch for stronger signs that the AI trade is maturing.

This could be "a slowdown in AI-related revenues for companies, or signs of less demand or less appetite for financing companies’ AI plans, be it through debt or through equity offerings," Rees told DW.

There are early signs that investors have less appetite for AI-related debt. Borrowing costs for AI infrastructure firms like CoreWeave and Oracle have soared recently. Even the cost of insuring Nvidia’s debt against default has risen 76% in a month, CNBC reported recently.

"They [Oracle] have been spending, some people say, like drunken sailors," Dick told DW. "They’ve compromised their balance sheet to a point where the stock’s fallen 65% from the highs."

That has not stopped Oracle, along with Meta, Microsoft and Alphabet, from continuing to issue new AI bonds. Since the end of last month, the four AI giants have announced deals worth $67 billion.

Rees said another sign could be any new regulations that make it harder to build out US data centers, due to pressure on local water and electricity supplies.

Is AI next in a long line of bubbles that burst?

In his upcoming book "AI Mania: Blather, Bluster, and the Bubble of All Bubbles," economist Gary Smith compares the AI boom with earlier frenzies around railways, automobiles, television and the internet. He warns of a "frightful crash" when the AI bubble eventually pops.

When the dot-com bubble burst in 2000, the tech-heavy Nasdaq stock market index lost nearly 80% of its value. Yet, previous bubbles have often lasted far longer than expected, making the timing of any crash hard to predict.

Joachim Klement, head of market strategy at UK-based investment bank Panmure Liberum, believes a reckoning could happen as early as next year.

"My core conviction is that the AI bubble will either burst in 2027 or in 2028, so sometime in the next two years,” Klement told Bloomberg last month.

Editor's note: This article was first published on November 13, 2026 and was updated on November 18 and 19 to reflect the latest developments.

articles.title: Quella di Anthropic è già la quotazione più grande di sempre
articles.summary: La società che sviluppa il chatbot Claude ha fissato il valore delle sue azioni a 83 dollari ciascuna
articles.preview: La società che sviluppa il chatbot Claude ha fissato il valore delle sue azioni a 83 dollari ciascuna Aggiornamento: nel frattempo Anthropic si è quotata in borsa, e il Post segue qui la quotazione Anthropic, la società di intelligenza artificiale (AI) che ha sviluppato il chatbot Claude, ha fissato a 83 dollari il prezzo delle azioni per la quotazione in borsa a New York di giovedì pomeriggio (ora italiana).
articles.body:
La società che sviluppa il chatbot Claude ha fissato il valore delle sue azioni a 83 dollari ciascuna

Aggiornamento: nel frattempo Anthropic si è quotata in borsa, e il Post segue qui la quotazione

Anthropic, la società di intelligenza artificiale (AI) che ha sviluppato il chatbot Claude, ha fissato a 83 dollari il prezzo delle azioni per la quotazione in borsa a New York di giovedì pomeriggio (ora italiana). Si tratta già in questa prima fase della più grande IPO (offerta pubblica iniziale di azioni) della storia: 83 dollari è il prezzo a cui sono state vendute in via preferenziale 980 milioni di azioni agli investitori – in questa fase perlopiù banche, fondi di investimento, e via così – e l’offerta è arrivata a un valore complessivo di 81,3 miliardi di dollari, attribuendo così all’intera società una valutazione di circa 1.500 miliardi di dollari.

Chi ha comprato queste azioni potrà rivenderle in borsa da oggi, quando all’apertura della borsa di New York – alle 15:30 ora italiana – le azioni di Anthropic inizieranno a essere negoziate sul mercato (e nello specifico al Nasdaq, il listino dei titoli tecnologici). Visto il grande entusiasmo per questa quotazione, con ogni probabilità il prezzo salirà ancora per la grande richiesta degli investitori, così anche il valore dell’intera società.

Il prezzo iniziale è comunque già superiore alle stime: la scorsa settimana la società aveva indicato un intervallo compreso tra 70 e 78 dollari per azione, ma le tante richieste degli investitori hanno portato su il prezzo. Per dimensioni, l’IPO supera quella di SpaceX, l’azienda spaziale e di comunicazioni satellitari di Elon Musk, che a giugno aveva raccolto 75 miliardi di dollari dagli investitori. Al momento della quotazione però SpaceX aveva una valutazione complessiva più alta: 1.770 miliardi di dollari.

Quella di Anthropic è una valutazione enorme per un’azienda nata appena cinque anni fa e che ancora non produce utili, anzi: dagli ultimi dati disponibili, nei primi nove mesi del 2026 ha registrato una perdita operativa di 1,3 miliardi di dollari. La perdita operativa mostra cosa si ottiene se dai ricavi si sottraggono i costi, ed è quindi l’indicatore che più mostra come va un’azienda nel suo business principale; secondo le regole contabili statunitensi però la perdita è persino più ampia, 104 miliardi di dollari, se si considerano particolari strumenti finanziari che, senza entrare troppo nei dettagli, l’azienda ha emesso per finanziare le sue attività ma che contribuiscono ad allargare il disavanzo.

Ciononostante Anthropic sta crescendo. Nei primi 9 mesi dell’anno ha ottenuto ricavi per 33 miliardi di dollari, molto superiori rispetto ai 4,6 miliardi di tutto il 2025. Il problema principale è se e quando questa crescita riuscirà a portare l’azienda a essere profittevole.

Un’altra particolarità della quotazione di Anthropic riguarda il poco potere decisionale che avranno le persone che ne compreranno le azioni, ovvero i futuri azionisti. In genere nelle aziende gli azionisti partecipano all’elezione dei membri del consiglio di amministrazione, l’organo che definisce le strategie di sviluppo societario. Anthropic, invece, ha creato una struttura organizzativa per cui gli azionisti avranno un potere molto limitato. Avviene lo stesso in altre aziende tecnologiche statunitensi.

La quotazione arriva in un momento delicato per le società del settore: la vittoria del Partito Democratico alle elezioni di metà mandato ha fatto aumentare tra gli investitori i timori di una maggiore regolamentazione, specialmente nello sviluppo dei data center; i recenti scandali che hanno coinvolto l’ex amministratore delegato di Nvidia Jensen Huang hanno creato problemi a una delle società più importanti del settore, col rischio che si espandano ad altre aziende; e da tempo molti osservatori si chiedono se non sia in corso una bolla speculativa.

L’andamento della quotazione di Anthropic è insomma un modo per analizzare a che punto è la maturazione del settore delle intelligenze artificiali e che valutazione ne danno analisti e investitori. Sarà inoltre osservato attentamente da OpenAI, l’azienda del chatbot ChatGPT e rivale di Anthropic, la cui quotazione dovrebbe avvenire nei prossimi mesi.

– Leggi anche: Anthropic può quotarsi senza farsi comandare dagli azionisti?
